items.title: Update: AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet
items.author: Baffoura30
items.body:
<!--- Please complete the sections below -->

## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The cheat sheet lists supply chain attacks as a key risk but has no guidance on third-party agent skills (SKILL.md packages loaded by Claude Code, Codex and similar agents). Skills are reviewed as files, but many tell the agent to read a page, download a script or run an installer hosted elsewhere. That remote content can change after review without the skill changing.

The [MCP Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/MCP_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html) already covers the equivalent problem for MCP tools (rug pulls, pinning reviewed definitions by hash). Skills have no equivalent guidance yet. The [OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agentic-skills-top-10) tracks this as AST05 (Untrusted External Instructions).

For context: I measured this in 355 popular public skills (disclosure: my own study, [doi:10.5281/zenodo.24209170](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24209170)). At least 36% explicitly tell the agent to read, download or run external content, and 13 of 4,273 external links were pinned.

## How should this be resolved?

Add a short "Third-Party Skills" subsection under Best Practices, plus matching Do's and Don'ts. Proposed points:

- Review a skill as its files plus everything it references: URLs, install commands and packages it tells the agent to fetch or run.
- Prefer bundling referenced instructions and scripts into the skill over fetching them at run time.
- Pin what can't be bundled: exact package versions, release URLs with checksums, and commit-hash links instead of branch links. Record a hash of fetched content at review and verify it before use or in CI.
- Re-review on every update, and fail CI on unapproved changes to the skill or its referenced content.
- Check for references hidden in HTML comments, encoded text or invisible characters.
- Avoid pipe-to-shell install steps in skills; use package managers or verified checksums.

References: OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 (AST05, AST07) and the existing MCP Security Cheat Sheet.

AI use: I drafted this with AI assistance and reviewed and edited it myself. I'm happy to submit the PR once the approach is agreed.

items.title: Update: Session Management Cheat Sheet - logout with an identity provider (small update)
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Session Management cheat sheet only covers local logout. Apps that sign users in through an IdP often keep their own session alive after the user logs out at the IdP or the IdP revokes the session, and there's no guidance on that. The SAML sheet has a single "define criteria for SAML logout" bullet, and the JWT sheet mentions logout tokens only as a `typ` example.

The specs cover the parts people get wrong. OIDC Back-Channel Logout (https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-backchannel-1_0.html) says how to validate a logout token (events claim, no nonce, jti, short exp) so it can't be replayed or confused with an ID token. RP-Initiated Logout (https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-rpinitiated-1_0.html) requires registered post-logout redirect URIs, which matters for open redirects. CAEP (https://openid.net/specs/openid-caep-1_0-final.html) defines session-revoked events.

## How should this be resolved?

Add a section on logout in federated setups: keep a mapping from the IdP session (sid/sub) to local sessions and end them server-side when a logout or revocation comes in, validate logout tokens per the spec, prefer back-channel over front-channel since third-party cookie blocking breaks the iframe approach, register exact post-logout redirect URIs, and keep local session lifetimes short as a backstop. Then cross-link it from the SAML and OAuth2 sheets. Happy to write this one if it gets the ack.

items.title: Update: OAuth2 Cheat Sheet - Device Authorization Grant and cross-device flows - RFC 8628 standard
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The OAuth2 cheat sheet doesn't cover the Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) or cross-device flows at all, and nothing else in the repo does either. Device code phishing is being used heavily in real attacks right now. The attacker starts a device flow, sends the victim the user code and the real login page, and gets tokens once the victim signs in. Microsoft's write-up on Storm-2372 is a good example (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/). RFC 8628 section 5 covers user code brute forcing and remote phishing, and RFC 10027 (BCP 247, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10027.html) now has best current practice for cross-device flows.

## How should this be resolved?

Add a short section to the OAuth2 sheet: only allow the device grant for clients that really are input-constrained and block it elsewhere (for example with conditional access), use short-lived, single-use, rate-limited user codes, show the client and device details on the consent screen, limit the scopes these clients can get, and prefer flows that prove the two devices are near each other where possible. I'm happy to open the PR if approved.

items.title: New CS proposal: Server-Side Document and Media Rendering
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is the proposed Cheat Sheet about?

Safely rendering untrusted content on the server: HTML-to-PDF engines (wkhtmltopdf, headless Chrome/Puppeteer), image tools like ImageMagick, Ghostscript and librsvg, ffmpeg, and office converters like LibreOffice. Most apps have an "export to PDF" or a thumbnailer somewhere, and these engines end up processing attacker-controlled input.

## What security issues are commonly encountered related to this area?

The renderer fetches whatever the document points at, so an iframe or image in user HTML becomes SSRF against internal services and cloud metadata (CVE-2022-35583 in wkhtmltopdf is a good example). file:// URLs and things like SVG xi:include lead to local file reads (CVE-2023-38633 in librsvg). ImageMagick delegates and coders have led to RCE (ImageTragick), and media and document converters bring their own protocol handlers and resource exhaustion. Right now the only coverage is one ImageTragick link and a re-encoding tip in the File Upload sheet. The SSRF sheet doesn't mention renderers as a source of outbound requests.

## What is the objective of the Cheat Sheet?

Give developers a short, engine by engine list of what to turn off and how to isolate it: disable JavaScript and network access in renderers or allowlist what they can load, block file:// and other schemes, use ImageMagick's policy.xml and ffmpeg's protocol whitelist, set resource limits, and run conversions in a sandboxed worker with no egress and a timeout. It would cross-link the File Upload, SSRF and XXE sheets.

## What other resources exist in this area?

ImageMagick's security policy docs (https://imagemagick.org/security-policy/), https://imagetragick.com/, CVE-2022-35583 (https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2022-35583), CVE-2023-38633, and the SSRF and File Upload cheat sheets, which touch this only in passing. I'd be happy to write it.

items.title: Update: Ruby on Rails Cheat Sheet - credentials key and Devise bcrypt cost (small update)
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

Two parts of the Ruby on Rails cheat sheet are out of date. The Sensitive Files list names `/config/initializers/secret_token.rb`, a file from before Rails 4.1, and doesn't mention `config/master.key`, which is the key that decrypts `config/credentials.yml.enc` in current Rails (https://guides.rubyonrails.org/security.html#custom-credentials). Committing that key is the mistake people actually make now.

The Encryption section also says Devise uses 10 stretches in production, but the current Devise initializer template defaults to a bcrypt cost of 12 (https://github.com/heartcombo/devise/blob/main/lib/generators/templates/devise.rb).

## How should this be resolved?

Replace `secret_token.rb` with `config/master.key` and `config/credentials/*.key`, and add a note that the encrypted credentials file can be committed but the keys can't. Update the Devise example to 12 and point to the Password Storage cheat sheet for bcrypt cost guidance. Will update if it gets ACKed!

items.author: cvas22

## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Kubernetes Security cheat sheet has a whole section on securing the Kubernetes Dashboard, including a note about versions before 1.8. The Dashboard project is now archived and no longer maintained, and its README points people to Headlamp, which moved under SIG UI (https://github.com/kubernetes/dashboard). The pre-1.8 note can go.  Will open PR if it gets ACK.

items.title: Update: Laravel Cheat Sheet - middleware examples for the bootstrap/app.php layout (small update)
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Laravel cheat sheet's middleware examples all assume the `App\Http\Kernel` class, which new apps don't have since Laravel 11. The cookie encryption section says to add `EncryptCookies` to the `web` group in `App\Http\Kernel`, the CSRF section talks about `VerifyCSRFToken` in the Kernel and excluding routes with the `$except` property, and the rate limiting section says to add `throttle` in `Kernel.php`.

Current Laravel registers middleware in `bootstrap/app.php`. The CSRF middleware is `ValidateCsrfToken`, it's in the `web` group by default, and exclusions go through `$middleware->validateCsrfTokens(except: [...])` (https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/csrf). The advice is still right, but someone on a new app can't follow the code as written.

## How should this be resolved?

Update those sections to the `bootstrap/app.php` / `withMiddleware()` API, using `validateCsrfTokens(except:)` and `encryptCookies(except:)`, and keep a short note for apps still on the old Kernel layout. I'm happy to open the PR.

items.title: Update: PHP Configuration Cheat Sheet - session settings deprecated in PHP 8.4
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The session block in the PHP Configuration cheat sheet sets `session.sid_length = 256` and `session.sid_bits_per_character = 6`, and the "paranoid checks" block sets `session.referer_check`. PHP 8.4 deprecated changing all three of these INI settings, so following the sheet on a current PHP version produces deprecation warnings and the settings are going away. See the Session section of https://www.php.net/manual/en/migration84.deprecated.php, which says to keep the default 32 character hex session IDs and stop changing `sid_length` and `sid_bits_per_character`.

A few other lines in the same file look stale too, like `mime_magic.magicfile` and some removed functions (`filepro*`, `dbase_open`) in the `disable_functions` list.

## How should this be resolved?

Drop the `sid_length`, `sid_bits_per_character` and `referer_check` lines and add a short note that the defaults are the supported setting from PHP 8.4 on, since the default ID already has enough entropy. While in there, clean up the settings and function names that no longer exist in supported PHP versions. I'm happy to open the PR.

items.title: Update: Input Validation Cheat Sheet - CRLF in response header values
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

Nothing in the series explains CRLF injection into HTTP response headers, also called response splitting (CWE-113). The pieces that exist are about other things. The Logging sheet covers CR and LF in log entries, the REST sheet has a single line saying services must defend against header injection, and the GraphQL sheet names CRLF in passing. None of them says what the attack does in a response (adding a `Set-Cookie`, rewriting a redirect `Location`, or ending the headers early to write a body), or what the developer should do about it.

It is a smaller risk than it used to be because most frameworks and servers now reject CR and LF in header values, but it still shows up where an app builds a header by hand or passes user input through to a proxy, a custom server, or an older runtime. The control is simple and worth stating once, so people don't have to guess whether their framework already handles it.

## How should this be resolved?

Add a short section to the Input Validation Cheat Sheet, next to the new "Host and Forwarded Headers" section, with the same size and style. It would say that user input written into a response header (redirect targets, cookie values, filenames in `Content-Disposition`, custom headers) must not contain CR, LF or NUL. Reject those values, or use the framework's header API, which refuses them, instead of building header lines by string concatenation. It would also say not to rely on encoding alone, and to check what a given framework does with such a value before assuming it is safe, and it would point to the Logging sheet for the log injection variant.

Sources would be RFC 9110 section 5.5 (field values containing CR, LF or NUL are invalid and dangerous, and a recipient must reject them or replace them with a space), CWE-113, the OWASP Community CRLF Injection page, and the WSTG test for HTTP splitting and smuggling. I'd read each one again before citing it.

I wasn't sure this earns a section of its own, so I'm raising it first. If you think it is too thin to add, or belongs in a different sheet such as HTTP Headers, happy to go with that. Will work on it and create a PR if this one get the ACK.

## Description

Adds a new `Secure Application Development Cheat Sheet` as a concise navigation hub for developers seeking security guidance throughout the application development lifecycle.

The Cheat Sheet organizes relevant OWASP guidance into five mentor-approved areas:

1. Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
2. Input Handling and Injection Prevention
3. Cryptography and Sensitive Data Protection
4. Application Architecture and Communication Boundaries
5. Dependencies, Deployment, and Security Operations

Each section briefly introduces key security considerations and links to relevant existing OWASP Cheat Sheets and authoritative external references. It also includes a light mapping to the OWASP Top 10:2025.

The document is intended as an entry point to existing OWASP guidance, not an exhaustive application security tutorial. It avoids duplicating detailed recommendations already covered by other Cheat Sheets.

timeline.message: docs: add Secure Application Development Cheat Sheet (#2805)

files.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,136 @@
+# Secure Application Development Cheat Sheet
+
+## Introduction
+
+This cheat sheet provides a concise entry point to the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series for developers designing and building applications. Rather than replicating in-depth implementation guidance or serving as an exhaustive manual, this guide helps development teams identify the security concerns that apply to their software architecture and directs them to authoritative OWASP Cheat Sheets for actionable practices.
+
+Modern application development requires embedding security across the entire software development lifecycle. The [OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/) provides an essential awareness document highlighting the most critical application security risks, while frameworks such as the [NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final) outline secure development practices. Each of the following sections addresses a core architectural domain, outlines when and why that domain matters, provides a light mapping to relevant [OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/) categories, and points to the relevant specialized cheat sheets.
+
+## 1. Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
+
+Identity, authentication, and access control establish who is interacting with an application—whether a human user or an automated service—and enforce what actions that subject is permitted to perform. These controls matter whenever an application manages sensitive assets, user accounts, multi-tenant boundaries, or service-to-service transactions. Inadequate controls allow attackers to impersonate legitimate entities, hijack active sessions, or execute unauthorized operations.
+
+**OWASP Top 10 Mapping:**
+
+- [A01:2025 – Broken Access Control](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/)
+- [A07:2025 – Authentication Failures](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A07_2025-Authentication_Failures/)
+
+**Relevant OWASP Cheat Sheets:**
+
+- **User Authentication and Credentials:**
+    - [Authentication Cheat Sheet](Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md): General authentication controls, password policies, and credential verification.
+    - [Password Storage Cheat Sheet](Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.md): Work-factor password hashing algorithms (Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt) and storage hygiene.
+    - [Multifactor Authentication Cheat Sheet](Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md): Multi-factor authentication (MFA) design and factor verification.
+    - [Passkey Security Cheat Sheet](Passkey_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md): Phishing-resistant passwordless authentication with WebAuthn and FIDO2.
+    - [Forgot Password Cheat Sheet](Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.md): Secure account recovery and credential reset flows.
+- **Session Management:**
+    - [Session Management Cheat Sheet](Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md): Session lifecycle, cookie security attributes, timeouts, and termination.
+    - [JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet](JSON_Web_Token_Cheat_Sheet.md): Cryptographic verification and claims handling for token-based sessions.
+- **Authorization and Access Control:**
+    - [Authorization Cheat Sheet](Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md): Principles of least privilege, default-deny authorization, and access enforcement.
+    - [Transaction Authorization Cheat Sheet](Transaction_Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md): Contextual step-up authorization and re-authentication for high-impact operations.
+- **Service Identities and Trust Boundaries:**
+    - [Workload Identity Federation Cheat Sheet](Workload_Identity_Federation_Cheat_Sheet.md): Machine identity federation without long-lived static credentials.
+    - [Identity Propagation Patterns Cheat Sheet](Identity_Propagation_Patterns_Cheat_Sheet.md): Propagating verified user context and calling service identity across microservices.
+
+## 2. Input Handling and Injection Prevention
+
+Input handling and injection defense govern how an application receives, inspects, processes, and displays data from untrusted sources. These controls matter whenever an application processes data from users, client requests, external APIs, webhooks, or file uploads. When applications process untrusted data without validation, parameterization, or context-aware encoding, attackers can manipulate query interpreters, execute unauthorized commands, or run malicious scripts in user browsers.
+
+**OWASP Top 10 Mapping:**
+
+- [A05:2025 – Injection](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A05_2025-Injection/)
+
+**Relevant OWASP Cheat Sheets:**
+
+- **Input Validation:**
+    - [Input Validation Cheat Sheet](Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.md): Allow-list validation strategies, syntactic checks, and semantic verification.
+- **Query Parameterization and Database Injections:**
+    - [Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet](Query_Parameterization_Cheat_Sheet.md): Prepared statements and parameterization to separate SQL code from untrusted data.
+    - [SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md): Defense-in-depth against SQL injection across relational database interfaces.
+- **Output Encoding and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS):**
+    - [Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet](Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md): Context-aware output encoding to prevent reflected and stored XSS.
+    - [DOM based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet](DOM_based_XSS_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md): Safe client-side JavaScript execution, sink defense, and DOM manipulation.
+- **Files, Payloads, and System Commands:**
+    - [File Upload Cheat Sheet](File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.md): File type validation, storage isolation, and safe handling of uploaded files.
+    - [XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet](XML_External_Entity_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md): Disabling external entity resolution and DTD processing in XML parsers.
+    - [OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet](OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.md): Safe argument handling and avoiding direct shell execution.
+    - [Deserialization Cheat Sheet](Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.md): Safe object serialization and preventing arbitrary code execution during deserialization.
+    - [Webhook Security Cheat Sheet](Webhook_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md): Verifying authenticity and payload integrity for incoming webhooks.
+
+## 3. Cryptography and Sensitive Data Protection
+
+Cryptography and sensitive data protection ensure the confidentiality and integrity of information both while moving across networks and while stored on disk. These controls matter whenever an application handles personal information, credentials, financial records, or operational secrets. Flaws in algorithm selection, encryption implementation, or credential storage can expose sensitive assets even if the rest of the application remains secure.
+
+**OWASP Top 10 Mapping:**
+
+- [A04:2025 – Cryptographic Failures](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A04_2025-Cryptographic_Failures/)
+
+**Relevant OWASP Cheat Sheets:**
+
+- **Transport Layer Security:**
+    - [Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet](Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md): Modern TLS protocol configuration, certificate validation, and secure channel setup.
+    - [HTTP Strict Transport Security Cheat Sheet](HTTP_Strict_Transport_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md): Enforcing encrypted HTTPS connections and preventing downgrade attacks.
+    - [Pinning Cheat Sheet](Pinning_Cheat_Sheet.md): Certificate and public key pinning for native applications and controlled endpoints.
+- **Data at Rest and Privacy:**
+    - [Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet](Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.md): Selecting vetted algorithms, encryption modes, and initialization vectors for data at rest.
+    - [User Privacy Protection Cheat Sheet](User_Privacy_Protection_Cheat_Sheet.md): Data minimization and privacy controls for personal data throughout its lifecycle.
+- **Secrets and Key Management:**
+    - [Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md): Safeguarding application credentials, API keys, vault integration, and rotation practices.
+    - [Key Management Cheat Sheet](Key_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md): Cryptographic key lifecycle management, including generation, storage, rotation, and destruction.
+
+## 4. Application Architecture and Communication Boundaries
+
+Application architecture and communication boundaries define how services interact with one another, how trust is partitioned, and how unexpected conditions are handled. These controls matter whenever applications expose APIs, communicate across network boundaries, integrate with third-party systems, or run behind reverse proxies. Without secure architecture defaults and explicit boundary defenses, applications are susceptible to request forgery, unintended exposure of internal topologies, and information disclosure through diagnostic messages.
+
+**OWASP Top 10 Mapping:**
+
+- [A01:2025 – Broken Access Control](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/)
+- [A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A02_2025-Security_Misconfiguration/)
+- [A06:2025 – Insecure Design](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A06_2025-Insecure_Design/)
+- [A10:2025 – Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A10_2025-Mishandling_of_Exceptional_Conditions/)
+
+**Relevant OWASP Cheat Sheets:**
+
+- **Outbound Request Protection:**
+    - [Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet](Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md): Destination host validation and network egress controls to prevent SSRF.
+- **API and Service Architecture:**

items.title: Update: HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet
items.author: SkillDMonkey
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Nginx subsection of the HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet explains `add_header ... always;` and (since #2952) how `add_header` is inherited, but it does not cover the most common Nginx deployment: Nginx as a reverse proxy in front of an application that already sends its own security headers.

`add_header` never replaces a header that comes from the upstream response: it appends a second copy. When the proxy and the application both set the same header, the client receives it twice, sometimes with different values. We measured this on one of our own sites during an internal assessment (nginx 1.26.3, reverse proxy, application sending its own headers):

```
x-frame-options: DENY
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
x-content-type-options: nosniff
...
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
x-frame-options: SAMEORIGIN
x-content-type-options: nosniff
```

Duplicated values are at best noise, and conflicting ones (here `DENY` and `SAMEORIGIN`) leave the effective policy unclear to anyone reading the configuration, and are reported as invalid by header scanners.

## How should this be resolved?

Add one short paragraph after the inheritance note in the Nginx subsection of `cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.md`:

> When Nginx proxies an application that already sends security headers, `add_header` does not replace them: the response carries both copies, possibly with conflicting values (for example `X-Frame-Options: DENY` from the application and `SAMEORIGIN` from Nginx). Set each header in one layer only, or drop the upstream copy with [`proxy_hide_header`](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_hide_header) before adding your own:
>
> ```nginx
> proxy_hide_header X-Frame-Options;
> add_header "X-Frame-Options" "DENY" always;
> ```

If this is welcome, I'd be glad to open the PR.

Prepared by an AI agent with the owner's permission.

+# HTTP Request Smuggling Prevention Cheat Sheet
+
+## Introduction
+
+Most applications sit behind at least one front-end component, such as a CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy, or web application firewall (WAF), that forwards requests to a back-end server over shared, reused connections. In this sheet, front end and back end mean these servers on the request path, the outbound and inbound sides in [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-3.7) terms, not browser code and server code. Both sides have to agree where each request ends. When they disagree, an attacker can send one request that the front end sees as a single request and the back end sees as two. The leftover part is prepended to whatever comes next on that connection, which may be another user's request ([RFC 9112: Request Smuggling](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-11.2), [CWE-444](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/444.html)).
+
+Depending on the application, this may let an attacker bypass access controls that only the front end enforces, capture other users' requests, and poison caches ([PortSwigger: Exploiting HTTP request smuggling](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling/exploiting#using-http-request-smuggling-to-bypass-front-end-security-controls)). The root cause is in how components parse message framing, so the defenses below are about removing ambiguity rather than filtering payloads.
+
+## How Desync Happens
+
+These are the common ways components end up disagreeing, not a complete list. More generally, any difference in how two components interpret a request, and so any lax parsing, can lead to request smuggling.
+
+- **Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding disagree.** An HTTP/1.1 request body is delimited either by `Content-Length` or by `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. If a request carries both, or a `Transfer-Encoding` value that one component accepts and another ignores, each side can pick a different length ([RFC 9112: Message Body Length](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-6.3)). [PortSwigger](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling#how-to-perform-an-http-request-smuggling-attack) calls these CL.TE and TE.CL, after which header each side uses, and TE.TE when both support `Transfer-Encoding` but one of them can be made to ignore an obfuscated version of it.
+- **HTTP/2 is downgraded to HTTP/1.1.** HTTP/2 frames carry their own length, but a front end that rewrites requests into HTTP/1.1 for the back end can pass along a `content-length` or `transfer-encoding` header, or a header value with a CR or LF in it, that then decides the framing on the back end ([PortSwigger: HTTP/2 desync attacks](https://portswigger.net/research/http2)).
+- **A server ignores a body it did not expect.** If the back end does not read the body of a request to an endpoint that normally has none, such as a static file or a redirect, the unread bytes are treated as the next request. Some of these cases can be triggered from a victim's browser, which poisons the browser's own connection to the site ([PortSwigger: Browser-powered desync attacks](https://portswigger.net/research/browser-powered-desync-attacks)).
+- **Line endings are parsed differently.** One component may accept a bare LF as the end of a line while another allows it inside a header value, so they see different headers, and a `Content-Length` hidden in one can frame the body in the other ([Zeyu: HTTP Request Smuggling in the Multiverse of Parsing Flaws](https://infosec.zeyu2001.com/2022/http-request-smuggling-in-the-multiverse-of-parsing-flaws)).
+
+## Prevention
+
+Most of these controls live in the proxy, load balancer or HTTP server rather than in application code. Administrators choose and configure those components so that they parse strictly, and the developers of those components implement the framing rules. Application developers mostly need to make sure the server reads every request body, closes connections on errors, and enforces authorization in the application itself.
+
+### Use HTTP/2 End-to-End
+
+Where the front end and the back end both support it, use HTTP/2 between them as well as towards clients, and turn off downgrading to HTTP/1.1. HTTP/2 determines the length of a request from its frames, so there is no second length to disagree about ([PortSwigger: How to prevent HTTP request smuggling](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling#how-to-prevent-http-request-smuggling-vulnerabilities)).
+
+### Reject Ambiguous HTTP/1.1 Framing
+
+Apply the framing rules from [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-6.1) in every component, and prefer the strict option where the specification allows a choice:
+
+- Reject a request that has both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding`. If a component processes it instead, it must use `Transfer-Encoding` alone. Either way, close the connection after responding.
+- Respond with `400 (Bad Request)` and close the connection when `Transfer-Encoding` is present and `chunked` is not the final coding.
+- Treat an invalid `Content-Length`, including several different values, as an unrecoverable error.
+- Respond with `400 (Bad Request)` and close the connection for a request with whitespace between a header field name and the colon (for example `Transfer-Encoding : chunked`), with obsolete line folding, or with a bare CR. A component that doesn't recognize such an obfuscated `Transfer-Encoding` header won't see it, which is how `TE.TE` slips past the rule above ([RFC 9112 section 5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-5.1), [section 5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-5.2), [section 2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-2.2)).
+
+Have the front end normalize or reject ambiguous requests, and have the back end reject any that are still ambiguous and close the connection ([PortSwigger](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling#how-to-prevent-http-request-smuggling-vulnerabilities)).
+
+### Validate Requests That Are Downgraded
+
+If HTTP/2 has to be translated to HTTP/1.1, validate the result as an HTTP/1.1 request before forwarding it ([RFC 9113: Field Validity](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-8.2.1)):
+
+- Treat an HTTP/2 request as malformed if a header value contains CR, LF, or NUL, or a header name contains a colon (other than the leading one of a pseudo-header), whitespace, or uppercase characters.
+- Treat an HTTP/2 request that contains `transfer-encoding` or other connection-specific headers as malformed ([RFC 9113: Connection-Specific Header Fields](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-8.2.2)).
+- Treat a `content-length` that does not match the length of the DATA frames as malformed ([RFC 9113: Malformed Messages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-8.1.1)).
+
+### Handle Connections Defensively
+
+- Read or discard the body of every request according to its declared length, even on endpoints that ignore the body. Never assume a request has no body ([PortSwigger](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling#how-to-prevent-http-request-smuggling-vulnerabilities)).
+- Close the connection instead of reusing it after a framing error or a server-level exception while handling a request.
+- Disabling the reuse of back-end connections limits some attacks but does not stop request tunneling and hurts performance, so it may not be worth it and should not be relied on alone.
+- Keep proxies, load balancers, and servers up to date, and check each product's own documentation for how it handles ambiguous requests and which settings make it strict.
+
+## What These Controls Do Not Cover
+
+- Request smuggling defeats controls that only the front end applies, because the smuggled request never passes through them. [RFC 9112 Section 11.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-11.2) describes this class of attack on message framing. Enforce authorization in the application as well, not only in the proxy or WAF.
+- A desync can poison a shared cache with another user's response. See the [Web Cache Security Cheat Sheet](Web_Cache_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md) for cache keys and what to cache.
+- Header injection through CR and LF in values the application writes into responses is a related but separate problem.
+
+## Testing
+
+Test through the same chain of CDN, load balancer, and proxies that production uses, since the bug is in how those components disagree. [PortSwigger](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling/finding#finding-http-request-smuggling-vulnerabilities-using-timing-techniques) describes timing-based probes. Some probes can disrupt other users' requests on a vulnerable system, so test in a non-production environment where possible.
+
+## References
+
+- [RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1, Section 6.3 Message Body Length](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-6.3)
+- [RFC 9113: HTTP/2, Section 8.2 HTTP Fields](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-8.2)
+- [CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/444.html)

 - Derive tenant and user identifiers from trusted, authenticated server-side context, not directly from an untrusted header or query parameter.
 - Apply the same URL normalization and parameter handling at the CDN, reverse proxy, and origin.

items.title: New CS proposal: HTTP Request Smuggling Prevention
items.author: cvas22
items.body:
## What is the proposed Cheat Sheet about?

An HTTP Request Smuggling Prevention cheat sheet. Nothing in the series covers it right now, not even in passing, even though most apps sit behind a CDN, load balancer or reverse proxy where front end and back end can disagree about where a request ends. The Web Cache Security sheet is the closest neighbor but it's about cache keys, not message framing.

## What security issues are commonly encountered related to this area?

- CL.TE, TE.CL and TE.TE desync when front end and back end parse `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` differently, or one ignores an obfuscated `Transfer-Encoding`
- HTTP/2 downgrade smuggling (H2.CL, H2.TE, CRLF in h2 header values) when the proxy rewrites HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 for the back end
- Back end connections shared across users, so a smuggled prefix gets attached to someone else's request (session theft, response queue poisoning)
- Bypassing front end access controls, WAF rules and auth headers added by the proxy
- Cache poisoning and stored XSS delivered through smuggled requests
- Client-side desync, where the browser itself is used to poison its own connection

## What is the objective of the Cheat Sheet?

Explain the root cause in plain terms and give concrete defenses: use HTTP/2 end to end where possible, have the front end normalize or reject ambiguous requests as RFC 9112 requires, don't reuse back end connections after a parsing error, keep proxy and server versions patched and on the same parsing rules, and know which settings matter in common proxies (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, cloud load balancers). Plus a short section on how to test for it and links to the Web Cache Security and HTTP Headers sheets.

## What other resources exist in this area?

- WSTG-INPV-15 Testing for HTTP Splitting Smuggling covers testing
- RFC 9112 section 6.3 (message body length) and RFC 9113 section 8.2.2 (h2 field validity)
- CWE-444 Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests
- PortSwigger's request smuggling research and Web Security Academy material

timeline.body:
Reviewed the rewrite against the sources it cites. Condensing the old certificate-pinning material is the right call, and the SPKI-hash guidance is correct across all three specs. Two places where the new text contradicts the sources it cites, both fixable with a sentence each.

### Must-fix 1 — "the only pinning mechanism on iOS"

> Use ATS pinning through `NSPinnedDomains` as the only pinning mechanism on iOS. Do not write custom server trust evaluation in a `URLSessionDelegate`; it is error-prone and offers no additional protection over a correctly configured `NSPinnedDomains` entry.

`NSPinnedDomains` only covers connections made through the URL Loading System, and this is documented in the MAS project that this PR is aligned with:

- [MASTG-KNOW-0072](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/knowledge/ios/MASVS-NETWORK/MASTG-KNOW-0072/) — "ATS pinning applies only to connections made via the URL Loading System (for example, `URLSession`). It doesn't apply to `Network` framework, `CFNetwork`, or BSD socket connections."
- [MASTG-BEST-0043](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/best-practices/MASTG-BEST-0043/) quotes Apple directly: "ATS doesn't apply to calls your app makes to lower-level networking interfaces like the `Network` framework or `CFNetwork`."

So for an app using `NWConnection`, `CFNetwork`, a bundled TLS stack, or a third-party SDK, declarative pinning is not in scope at all, and explicit `SecTrust` evaluation is the only way to pin. Two further cases where the absolute claim fails:

- **Frameworks and SDKs** cannot write the host app's `Info.plist`, so they cannot rely on `NSPinnedDomains` — this is the case TrustKit (removed by this PR) exists for.
- **Deployment targets below iOS 14 / macOS 11**, where `NSPinnedDomains` does not exist.

Suggested replacement, which keeps the preference without the false universality:

> Prefer ATS pinning through `NSPinnedDomains` for connections made through the URL Loading System (`URLSession`, `WKWebView`): it is declarative, auditable, and enforced by the system. ATS does not cover lower-level interfaces (Network.framework, CFNetwork, BSD sockets) or bundled third-party TLS stacks; those require explicit `SecTrust` evaluation, which is error-prone and should be confined to the code that needs it.

If that replacement goes in, the TrustKit citation becomes useful again as the maintained alternative to hand-rolled evaluation.

### Must-fix 2 — leaf-primary contradicts Apple and MAS

Three statements now disagree with each other and with the cited guidance:

- "Apple ... recommends pinning CA public keys with backups rather than a single leaf key."
- **Recommendation:** "pin the leaf or issuing CA public key as the primary pin".
- "Pinning the root CA ... Use it only as a backup pin, not as the primary pin."

Apple's [Identity Pinning](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=g9ejcf8y) states that a pinned CA key "must appear in a certificate chain either in an intermediate or root certificate", and [MASTG-KNOW-0072](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/knowledge/ios/MASVS-NETWORK/MASTG-KNOW-0072/) says `NSPinnedCAIdentities` "pins an intermediate or root CA's public key" and that "pinning to a CA is more resilient to certificate renewals". Android's documentation makes the same trade-off.

A root-CA pin is the most rotation-tolerant option available. "Backup only" is a defensible *risk* position, but as written it reads as a technical rule and directly contradicts the sentence two paragraphs above it. Please pick one and state the trade-off, for example:

> Pin a CA public key (intermediate or root) as the primary identity, with at least one backup CA pin. CA pins survive certificate renewal, which is why Apple and Android recommend them; the cost is that you still trust everything that CA issues. Leaf pinning narrows trust further, but must be treated as breakage-on-renewal unless you control rotation.

### Nit — "same CSR"

> ... this stays the same if the same Certificate Signing Request (CSR) is used.

What stays constant is the **key pair**. A reissued certificate keeps the SPKI when it is issued for the same key, whether or not the CSR is reused. Suggest "if the certificate is reissued for the same key pair".

### Checked and fine

- The SPKI/SHA-256 claim is correct for all three formats: RFC 7469 §2.4 defines the pin as `base64(SHA-256(SPKI))`, Android's `<pin digest="SHA-256">` hashes the SPKI, and Apple's `SPKI-SHA256-BASE64` is the same digest.
- I searched every Markdown file in the repo for links into this sheet: nothing links to `#certificate`, `#public-key`, or `#hash`, so removing those headings does not break any inbound anchors.
- The new MAS links resolve (200): MASTG-KNOW-0015, MASTG-TECH-0012, MASTG-TECH-0064, MASWE-0028.

> *🤖 **Automated LLM review (multi-model).** This review was written by language models and may be wrong. Please double-check every point; you do not have to agree with it.*

Thanks @sushi2k, aligning the sheet with OWASP MAS is the right direction, all 24 links check out, and both of Skeletor-Pirate's must-fixes (ATS scope, CA-primary pinning) and the "same key pair" nit are resolved. A few correctness issues came up in the rewrite:

1. **iOS leaf + backup CA pin doesn't work as a backup.** Per [Apple's NSPinnedDomains docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/information-property-list/nsapptransportsecurity/nspinneddomains), when both `NSPinnedLeafIdentities` and `NSPinnedCAIdentities` are set, ATS requires a match in *each* category, so the CA pin is an extra requirement and the app breaks on the first leaf-key rotation. The sheet itself says this on the iOS line, which contradicts the "always pair a leaf pin with a backup CA pin" advice. On iOS, the backup for a leaf pin must be another leaf key; "leaf + backup CA" only works with any-match pinsets (Android Network Security Configuration, OkHttp, TrustKit).
2. **TrustKit is overstated.** Its automatic mode only swizzles `NSURLSession`/`NSURLConnection` delegates, which ATS already covers ([MASTG-KNOW-0072](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/knowledge/ios/MASVS-NETWORK/MASTG-KNOW-0072/)). It does not cover the Network framework or bundled TLS stacks on its own. Please narrow the claim.
3. **OpenSSL steps pin only the leaf.** `SSL_get1_peer_certificate` returns only the end-entity certificate, which contradicts the CA-primary recommendation. Please require `SSL_VERIFY_PEER` and hostname checking with `SSL_set1_host`, and match pins against `SSL_get0_verified_chain()`, never `SSL_get_peer_cert_chain()`, which is [not a verified chain](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get_peer_cert_chain/).
4. **Electron steps pin only the leaf and don't say how to accept.** Please match pins against `request.validatedCertificate` and its `issuerCert` chain, and accept with `callback(-3)`, because `callback(0)` disables Certificate Transparency verification ([Electron: setCertificateVerifyProc](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/session#sessetcertificateverifyprocproc)).
5. **Default stance is missing.** Android ("not recommended for Android apps"), Apple ("in most cases, pinning is not necessary and should be avoided") and the OWASP page the sheet cites all say most apps shouldn't pin. Please restore an explicit "most apps should not pin" near the top.
6. **Process:** the PR body is the unfilled template. Please add a short description of what changed and why (certificate/hash pinning removed, TrustKit and Electron changes, sample `.zip` files dropped), and link a tracking issue, since this rewrites about half the sheet. Please also paste the actual prompt in the AI disclosure instead of a summary.

Source material for the open points, since two of the three citations are awkward to quote from: Apple's page renders through JavaScript, and OpenSSL's `SSL_get0_verified_chain` page is empty.

**Apple — `NSPinnedDomains`**

From Apple's documentation for the key:

> "For any domain that you specify, you must include one or more expected Certificate Authority (CA) or sub-CA certificates as the value for the key, one or more expected leaf certificates as the value for the key, or both. If you specify both, App Transport Security (ATS) requires a match in each category."

The page is client-rendered, so that text is not in the raw HTML; it is at the URL the sheet already links.

So "always pair it with a backup CA pin" does not hold on iOS: the CA pin becomes a second requirement rather than a fallback, and the app breaks on the first leaf-key rotation. The backup for a leaf pin there is a second entry in `NSPinnedLeafIdentities`, since ATS accepts a match against any entry within a category. "Leaf plus backup CA" only works where the pinset is any-match — Android's `<pin-set>`, OkHttp's `CertificatePinner`, TrustKit.

**OpenSSL — verified chain**

From [`SSL_get_peer_cert_chain(3)`](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get_peer_cert_chain/):

> "NB: `SSL_get_peer_cert_chain()` returns the peer chain as sent by the peer: it only consists of certificates the peer has sent (in the order the peer has sent them) it is not a verified chain. `SSL_get0_verified_chain()` returns the verified certificate chain of the peer including the peer's end entity certificate. It must be called after a session has been successfully established. If peer verification was not successful (as indicated by `SSL_get_verify_result()` not returning `X509_V_OK`) the chain may be incomplete or invalid."

One practical caveat if that gets linked: `https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get0_verified_chain/` returns HTTP 200 but renders an empty page, so it is not usable as a citation target — the sentence above lives in the `SSL_get_peer_cert_chain(3)` page. For the hostname check, [`SSL_set1_host`](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_set1_host/) documents the name parameters, including `X509_CHECK_FLAG_NO_PARTIAL_WILDCARDS`.

**Electron — accept value**

From [`ses.setCertificateVerifyProc`](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/session#sessetcertificateverifyprocproc), the `verificationResult` values the callback accepts:

> "`0` - Indicates success and disables Certificate Transparency verification.
> `-2` - Indicates failure.
> `-3` - Uses the verification result from chromium."

So `callback(0)` is what turns Certificate Transparency off, and `callback(-3)` keeps Chromium's verification and layers the pin check on top of it. The request object carries both `certificate` and `validatedCertificate`, and Electron's `Certificate` has an `issuerCert` property ("Issuer certificate (if not self-signed)"), so the chain to match against is `request.validatedCertificate` and its `issuerCert`.

-Pinning is the process of associating a host with their *expected* X509 certificate or public key. If more than one certificate or public key is acceptable, then the program holds a *pinset* (taken from [Jon Larimer and Kenny Root Google I/O talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RPJENzweI-A)). In this case, the advertised credential must match one of the elements in the pinset.
-
-### When to Add a Pin
+Pinning is the process of associating a host with its *expected* X.509 public key. Once a public key is known or seen for a host, the public key is associated or 'pinned' to the host. If more than one public key is acceptable, the set of acceptable keys is called a *pinset*, and the server's public key must match one of them.
 
-A host or service's certificate or public key can be added to an application at development time, it can be added upon first encountering the certificate or public key (an approach commonly known as “Trust On First Use”, or TOFU), or it can be added and updated in real time via an unpinned channel. +### Android
 
-To enable pinning, [the `<pin-set>` configuration setting](https://developer.android.com/training/articles/security-config.html#CertificatePinning) can be used.
+Since Android 7.0 (API level 24), the preferred way to implement pinning is the [Network Security Configuration](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/security-config), a declarative XML file that applies to all framework-managed traffic without app code.

+### .NET

-Pinning can occur at one of two places with OpenSSL. First is the user supplied `verify_callback`. Second is after the connection is established via `SSL_get_peer_certificate`. Either method will allow you to access the peer's certificate.
-

+OpenSSL has no declarative pinning mechanism. -1. You must call `SSL_get_verify_result` and verify the return code is `X509_V_OK`;

After the handshake:
 
-Download: [OpenSSL sample program](../assets/Pinning_Cheat_Sheet_Certificate_OpenSSLSample.zip).
+1. Call `SSL_get_verify_result` and verify the return code is `X509_V_OK`;

-
-Otherwise, you can validate certificates by yourself using [ses.setCertificateVerifyProc(proc)](https://electronjs.org/docs/api/session#sessetcertificateverifyprocproc).

Validate server certificates with [`ses.setCertificateVerifyProc(proc)`](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/session#sessetcertificateverifyprocproc), which Electron calls for every server certificate verification in that session. ## What is missing or needs to be updated?
The [Django_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md](https://github.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries/blob/master/cheatsheets/Django_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md) currently lacks a consolidated, secure-by-default `settings.py` configuration example that shows how to enforce production security settings by default while overriding them safely in a local `.env` environment. It also misses practical settings like `__Host-` cookie prefixes, `SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY`, `SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY`, and a complete `SECURE_CSP` (Django 6.0+) dictionary example.

## How should this be resolved?
Add an **Application security configuration** section before the Admin panel URL section containing:
- A fail-safe `settings.py` snippet using `django-environ` and `django.utils.csp` where HTTPS redirects, HSTS, security headers, `__Host-` cookies, and CSP are enabled by default.
- A corresponding `.env` snippet showing which parameters to override for local development without HTTPS.

I have already prepared and submitted the implementation in PR #2970.

items.body:
Adds a short "Docker Swarm" subsection at the end of Rule #5a, covering both #2936 and #2951 in one PR as requested by the maintainer.

- #2936: Option 1 (binding to `127.0.0.1`) does not apply to Swarm services. A published service port cannot be bound to a host IP ([moby/moby#26696](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/26696)); with the routing mesh it listens on every IP of every node, and `mode=host` still opens it on all interfaces of the node running the task. Services that only talk to other services should use an overlay network instead of being published; otherwise the remaining control on the node is the `DOCKER-USER` chain.
- #2951: the Swarm ports (7946/tcp+udp and 4789/udp on every node, 2377/tcp on managers) should be allowed only from the other Swarm nodes; overlay traffic is unencrypted by default and VXLAN is unauthenticated ([GHSA-vwm3-crmr-xfxw](https://github.com/moby/moby/security/advisories/GHSA-vwm3-crmr-xfxw)); `--opt encrypted` on untrusted links, with the caveats of CVE-2023-28840 and CVE-2023-28842.

As asked in #2951, there are no firewall rule sets or scripts, only links to the Docker documentation and the moby advisories.

- Every sentence was checked against the linked source by a second agent, starting from the text only.

  - ingress ports are DNATed for every local address (`PREROUTING -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL`);

One ingress service was published 8081 → target 80 and one `mode=host` service 8082 → target 80. Each row is a DROP rule in `DOCKER-USER`, then curl from the client:

| rule in `DOCKER-USER` | ingress 8081 → 80 | `mode=host` 8082 → 80 |
|---|---|---|
| none | 200 | 200 |
| `-p tcp --dport 80` (target port) | 200, not blocked | blocked |
| `-p tcp --dport 8081` / `--dport 8082` (published port) | blocked | 200, not blocked |
| `-p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8081` / `8082` | blocked | blocked |

 Refer to the [Docker and iptables documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/packet-filtering-firewalls/) for a deeper explanation of how Docker interacts with the host firewall.
 
+#### Docker Swarm
+
+Option 1 does not apply to Swarm services: a port published with `docker service create --publish` or `docker stack deploy` cannot be bound to a single host IP ([moby/moby#26696](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/26696)).
+
+- **Publishing:** with the default ingress routing mesh, the published port listens on every IP address of every node in the swarm ([Docker docs, routing mesh](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/ingress/)); `mode=host` bypasses the routing mesh but still opens the port on all interfaces of the node that runs the task. A service that only needs to be reached by other services should not be published: attach it to an overlay network (optionally [`--internal`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/network/create/)) and reach it by service name.
+- **Firewall:** if a service must be published, the remaining control on the node is the host firewall. Inbound IPv4 traffic for both publishing modes is NATed, so filter it in the [`DOCKER-USER` chain](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/firewall-iptables/#add-iptables-policies-before-dockers-rules) and match the published port with conntrack's `--ctorigdstport` ([match the original IP and ports](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/firewall-iptables/#match-the-original-ip-and-ports-for-requests)), which works for both modes, or match the incoming interface or source. Do not rely on `--dport`: in `DOCKER-USER` it sees the container port for `mode=host` but the published port for the ingress routing mesh, which rewrites the port later inside the task's network namespace, so a rule written on the wrong port matches nothing and leaves the service exposed.
+- **IPv6:** the path depends on the task's network. If the network has no IPv6, the userland proxy serves a `mode=host` port on the host's IPv6 addresses ([port publishing](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/port-publishing/)) and that traffic goes through the `INPUT` chain. If the network has IPv6 and `ip6tables` is enabled, Docker NATs it as well and it is filtered in the ip6tables `DOCKER-USER` chain. Check which path your hosts use (DNAT rules in `ip6tables -t nat -S`) and filter that one.
+- **Ports between nodes:** by default Swarm listens on 7946/tcp+udp (node discovery) and 4789/udp (overlay network traffic, VXLAN) on every node, and on 2377/tcp (cluster management) on manager nodes; 4789 can be changed with `docker swarm init --data-path-port` and 2377 with `--listen-addr`. Allow the ports your swarm actually uses only from the other Swarm nodes ([Docker docs, overlay network ports](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/overlay/), [Swarm networking](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/networking/)).
+- **Overlay encryption:** overlay traffic is not encrypted by default and VXLAN has no authentication, so an open 4789/udp lets anyone who can reach it inject Ethernet frames into overlay networks ([GHSA-vwm3-crmr-xfxw](https://github.com/moby/moby/security/advisories/GHSA-vwm3-crmr-xfxw)). When nodes communicate over untrusted links, create overlay networks with `--opt encrypted`, allow IP protocol 50 (ESP) between the nodes, and still never accept 4789/udp from untrusted sources.
+- **The `ingress` network is not covered:** `--opt encrypted` applies only to the network it is set on; the default `ingress` network used by the routing mesh stays unencrypted unless it is [recreated with encryption](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/networking/#customize-ingress).
+- **Vulnerable versions:** before Docker Engine 23.0.3 and 20.10.24, encrypted overlay networks could silently accept cleartext VXLAN packets, for example when the `xt_u32` kernel module was missing or on a node with a single endpoint ([CVE-2023-28840](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-232p-vwff-86mp), [CVE-2023-28842](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wrf-mxfj-pf5p)).
+

 **First of all, do not disable default security profile!** Always start with Docker’s or your host’s default profile as a baseline.

items.title: Update: Docker Security Cheat Sheet (Swarm ports and unencrypted overlay VXLAN)
items.author: SkillDMonkey
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Docker Security Cheat Sheet (rule #1 covers the TCP daemon socket) says nothing about the ports Docker Swarm opens on every node: 2377/tcp (cluster management), 7946/tcp+udp (gossip) and 4789/udp (VXLAN data plane of overlay networks). They listen on all interfaces regardless of `--advertise-addr`, Docker gives no warning about it, and the host firewall INPUT chain is the only thing in front of them.

Moby's own advisories say that unencrypted overlay traffic on UDP 4789 accepts packets from anyone who can reach the port, so a host on the same network can inject packets into container overlay networks, and recommend closing 4789 to untrusted traffic ([GHSA-vwm3-crmr-xfxw](https://github.com/moby/moby/security/advisories/GHSA-vwm3-crmr-xfxw)). Overlay networks are unencrypted unless created with `--opt encrypted`, and the encrypted mode has its own caveats ([CVE-2023-28840 / GHSA-232p-vwff-86mp](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-232p-vwff-86mp), [CVE-2023-28842 / GHSA-6wrf-mxfj-pf5p](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wrf-mxfj-pf5p)). It can be checked on any Swarm node with `ss -tulnp`.

## How should this be resolved?

A short rule in the cheat sheet:

- allow 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp and 4789/udp only from the other Swarm nodes (or only on the interface used for `--advertise-addr`), and drop them from every other source;
- use `--opt encrypted` for overlay networks that carry sensitive traffic when nodes are not on a trusted or already encrypted link, keeping in mind the advisories above;
- link the Docker docs on [Swarm networking](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/networking/) and the moby advisories.

Single file, a few added lines. We are happy to be assigned and to open the pull request referencing this issue.

AI disclosure: this issue was written and submitted by an AI agent (Claude Opus 5.5) on behalf of Unitizy, with the owner's permission. A second agent checked every claim against the moby advisories and the Docker documentation linked above.

Keep it to a short note: restrict 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp and 4789/udp to the other Swarm nodes, and use `--opt encrypted` on untrusted links with the caveats from the advisories. No firewall rule sets or scripts; link the Docker Swarm networking docs instead.

Checked the new section against the linked MDN pages (the header reference, the CORS guide's *Requests with credentials* and *Credentialed requests and wildcards* sections) and the Fetch standard's credential model. The core statements are correct:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` has exactly one valid value, `true`.
- A credentialed response with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is blocked by the browser even when `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is present.
- Validating `Origin` against an explicit allowlist and emitting `Vary: Origin` when the response reflects it is the right caching-safe advice.
- The preflight/subsequent-request note is right: the preflight itself carries no cookies or HTTP auth, but once the actual request is credentialed, the preflight response must include `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
- `SameSite=None; Secure` and "CORS is not CSRF protection" are both correct and worth having here.

**One gap worth closing.** The wildcard prohibition is stated only for `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. For credentialed requests the same rule applies to three more headers: `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` must each return an explicit list, not `*` (MDN, *Credentialed requests and wildcards*). This is the most common credentialed-CORS failure after the ACAO wildcard, and a reader who follows this section could easily emit:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://trusted-site.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: *
```

and get a CORS error with no obvious cause. One bullet under **Recommendation** naming the three headers would cover it.

**One precision nit.** "CORS preflight requests do not include credentials" is true for cookies and HTTP authentication, but not for TLS client certificates: MDN notes Chromium currently always sends TLS client certificates in CORS preflight requests (Chrome bug 775438), and Firefox does so conditionally (bug 1511151). Since the paragraph above explicitly lists TLS client certificates as credentials, the blanket wording contradicts it slightly. Suggest "preflight requests do not carry cookies or HTTP authentication credentials (some browsers may still attach TLS client certificates)".

**Template:** the sourcing checkbox is malformed — `- []` renders as literal text rather than a checkbox; it needs `- [x]` (most claims do have inline MDN citations, but a couple, e.g. the single-valid-value statement, lean on the linked header page, so it is worth a final pass against the source you cite).

The section is in the right place structurally (sibling of `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, before COOP) and reads well. Fix the wildcard gap and this is mergeable from my side.

Thanks for fixing the checkbox, and for taking the TLS point seriously.

On the wildcard: your structural reasoning is fair — this page documents one header per section, and it should not turn into an ACAH/ACAM tutorial. But the restriction I raised isn't a preflight *topic*; it's keyed to the **actual request's credentials mode**, which is exactly the case your section documents. The preflight response is just where those headers happen to be returned.

Fetch standard §3.3.5, *CORS protocol and credentials*:

> Similarly, `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` response headers can only use `*` as value when request's credentials mode is not `"include"`.

And MDN, *Credentialed requests and wildcards*:

> When responding to a credentialed request: ... The server must not specify the `*` wildcard for the `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` response-header value ... [same for `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`].

So a service doing exactly what this section recommends — `credentials: "include"` plus an explicit origin — still fails if its preflight response returns `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` or `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: *`. That is the most common follow-on bug after the ACAO one, and the reader has no pointer to it anywhere else in the sheet, because those headers have no section of their own.

If you want to keep it to one bullet and avoid defining the other headers, this is enough:

> - The same wildcard restriction applies to the other CORS response headers: for credentialed requests, list header and method names explicitly in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` and `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and names explicitly in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, rather than using `*`.

That's configuration advice about credentialed CORS, not a description of ACAH/ACAM. But it is still a scope call, so if you or the maintainers would rather keep the section strictly about this one header, say so and I'll drop it — no objection either way.

On the TLS nit, the exact source is the *Preflight requests and credentials* note in the same MDN CORS guide: the spec says preflights must never include credentials, but "Chromium-based browsers currently always send TLS client certificates in CORS preflight requests (Chrome bug 775438)", and Firefox allows it behind `network.cors_preflight.allow_client_cert` (Firefox bug 1511151) for enterprise auth. So the accurate version keeps your sentence and adds the caveat, e.g.:

> CORS preflight requests must not include credentials. Some browsers nonetheless attach TLS client certificates to preflight requests for enterprise authentication (Chromium always does; Firefox behind a preference), so treat the preflight as credential-free for cookies and HTTP authentication only.

 ## 2 General Secrets Management
 
-The following sections address the main concepts relating to secrets management.
+Secrets management relies on foundational principles spanning lifecycle governance, least-privilege access, automated rotation, and runtime memory protection to prevent credential compromise and limit breach impact.
 
 ### 2.1 High Availability
 
-It is vital to select a technology that is robust enough to service traffic reliably:
-
-- Users (e.g., SSH keys, root account passwords). In an incident response scenario, users expect to be provisioned with credentials rapidly, so they can recover services that have gone offline. Having to wait for credentials could impact the responsiveness of the operations team.
-- Applications (e.g., database credentials and API keys). If the service is not performant, it could degrade the availability of dependent applications or increase application startup times.
-
-Such a service could receive a considerable volume of requests within a large organization.
+Secrets management systems sit on the critical path for both application availability and operational recovery. Latency or outages in secrets infrastructure degrade dependent services, delay application startup, and impede incident responders retrieving emergency credentials. Deploy secrets management solutions with clustering, multi-region replication, and automated failover capable of reliably serving production traffic and disaster-recovery operations.
 
 ### 2.2 Centralize and Standardize
 
-Secrets used by your DevOps teams for your applications might be consumed differently than secrets stored by your marketeers or your SRE team. You often find poorly maintained secrets where the needs of secret consumers or producers mismatch. Therefore, you must standardize and centralize the secrets management solution with care. Standardizing and centralizing can mean that you use multiple secret management solutions. For instance: your cloud-native development teams choose to use the solution provided by the cloud provider, while your private cloud uses a third-party solution, and everybody has an account for a selected password manager.
-By making sure that the teams standardize the interaction with these different solutions, they remain maintainable and usable in the event of an incident.
-Even when a company centralizes its secrets management to just one solution, you will often have to secure the primary secret of that secrets management solution in a secondary secrets management solution. For instance, you can use a cloud provider's facilities to store secrets, but that cloud provider's root/management credentials need to be stored somewhere else.
-
-Standardization should include Secrets life cycle management, Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting of the secrets management solution, and life cycle management. Note that it should be immediately apparent to an organization what a secret is used for and where to find it. The more Secrets management solutions you use, the more documentation you need.
+Centralizing secrets storage reduces secret sprawl and enables uniform enforcement of lifecycle, access, and auditing policies. Where multi-cloud or hybrid architectures necessitate multiple specialized stores (such as cloud-native vaults alongside container secrets stores), standardize naming conventions, authentication mechanisms, and access patterns across platforms. Maintain clear documentation of secret ownership and purpose. The primary administrative and root credentials of the secrets management platform itself must be secured in an independent, secondary storage mechanism to prevent single points of administrative compromise.
 
 ### 2.3 Access Control
 
-When users can read and/or update the secret in a secret management system, it means that the secret can now leak through that user and the system they used to touch the secret.
-Therefore, engineers should not have access to all secrets in the secrets management system, and the Least Privilege principle should be applied. The secret management system needs to provide the ability to configure fine-grained access controls on each object and component to accomplish the Least Privilege principle.
+Enforce the principle of least privilege across all secrets infrastructure. Limit human and machine access using fine-grained, path-based access control policies scoped strictly to the specific secrets and operations required for each workload or operational role. Separate administrative roles managing the secrets platform from consumer roles reading credentials. Restrict and audit direct human access to production secrets, preferring automated delivery wherever possible.
 
 ### 2.4 Automate Secrets Management
 
-Manual maintenance not only increases the risk of leakage; it also introduces the risk of human errors while maintaining the secret. Furthermore, it can become wasteful.
-Therefore, it is better to limit or remove the human interaction with the actual secrets. You can restrict human interaction in multiple ways:
+Automating secret provisioning and rotation eliminates error-prone manual interventions and limits human exposure to plaintext credentials:
 
-- **Secrets pipeline:** Having a secrets pipeline that does large parts of the secret management (e.g., creation, rotation, etc.)
-- **Using dynamic secrets:** When an application starts, it could request its database credentials, which, when dynamically generated, will be provided with new credentials for that session. Dynamic secrets should be used where possible to reduce the surface area of credential reuse. Configure a short [lease duration](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/lease) and revoke credentials when they are no longer needed. Restarting the application does not itself revoke stolen credentials; they remain usable until the backing service expires or revokes them.
-- **Automated rotation of static secrets:** Key rotation is a challenging process when implemented manually, and can lead to mistakes. It is therefore better to automate the rotation of keys or at least ensure that the process is sufficiently supported by IT.
-
-Rotating certain keys, such as encryption keys, might trigger full or partial data re-encryption. Different strategies for rotating keys exist:
-
-- Gradual rotation
-- Introducing new keys for Write operations
-- Leaving old keys for Read operations
-- Rapid rotation
-- Scheduled rotation
-- and more...
+- **Automated Delivery Pipelines:** Integrate secrets provisioning into deployment pipelines and runtime orchestrators so secrets are delivered directly to workloads without manual extraction.
+- **Dynamic Secrets:** Where supported by backing services (such as databases or cloud platforms), generate ephemeral credentials dynamically on demand for each workload session. Dynamic secrets significantly reduce the blast radius of credential theft. Configure short [lease durations](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/lease) and explicitly revoke credentials when no longer needed; restarting a client process does not revoke credentials issued by the backing service.
+- **Risk-Based Automated Rotation:** Implement automated rotation for static credentials and cryptographic keys to reduce the window of opportunity for exposed secrets. Rotation frequency should align with credential privilege, exposure surface, provider lease policies, and operational risk rather than an arbitrary calendar schedule. Automated rotation must be triggered immediately upon suspected compromise.
 
 #### 2.4.1 Architectural Patterns for Automated Rotation
 
-To illustrate how to design systems that support automated secret rotation, here are a few architectural patterns:
-
-##### Example 1: Kubernetes with a Sidecar Container
-
-In a Kubernetes environment, a common pattern is to use a sidecar container that is responsible for retrieving secrets from a secrets manager and making them available to the main application container. This decouples the application from the specifics of the secrets management solution.
-
-- **Architecture:**
-    - A Pod contains two containers: the main application container and a sidecar container (e.g., HashiCorp Vault Agent, CyberArk Conjur Secrets Provider).
-    - The sidecar container authenticates with the secrets manager (e.g., using a Kubernetes Service Account).
-    - It retrieves the secret and writes it to a shared in-memory volume.
-    - The application container reads the secret from the shared volume.
-    - The sidecar container can periodically refresh the secret, ensuring the application always has a valid, short-lived credential.
-- **Kubernetes Manifest Snippet:**
-
-    ```yaml
-    apiVersion: v1
-    kind: Pod
-    metadata:
-      name: my-app
-    spec:
-      serviceAccountName: my-app-sa
-      containers:
-      - name: my-app-container
-        image: my-app-image
-        volumeMounts:
-        - name: secrets-volume
-          mountPath: "/mnt/secrets"
-          readOnly: true
-      - name: vault-agent-sidecar
-        image: vault:latest
-        args: ["agent", "-config=/etc/vault/vault-agent-config.hcl"]
-        volumeMounts:
-        - name: secrets-volume
-          mountPath: "/mnt/secrets"
-      volumes:
-      - name: secrets-volume
-        emptyDir:
-          medium: "Memory"
-    ```
-
-##### Example 2: Serverless Function for Database Credential Rotation
-
-Cloud-native secret managers often provide built-in support for automated rotation using serverless functions (e.g., AWS Lambda, Azure Functions).
-
-- **Architecture:**
-    - A secret is stored in a cloud secrets manager (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager).
-    - The secrets manager is configured to trigger a rotation Lambda function on a schedule.
-    - The Lambda function has the necessary permissions to update the database password and the secret value in the secrets manager.
-    - The rotation process typically involves multiple steps (create new secret, set new secret, test new secret, finish rotation) to ensure a safe transition.
-
-For AWS, start from the [rotation function templates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/reference_available-rotation-templates.html). Secrets Manager invokes the function [separately for each rotation step](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotate-secrets_lambda.html); retrieve the pending credential from the secret version identified by `ClientRequestToken`, rather than relying on a local variable from an earlier invocation.
-
-Follow the [rotation function security checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotate-secrets_lambda-functions.html) and [template validation](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-secrets-manager-rotation-lambdas/blob/master/SecretsManagerRotationTemplate/lambda_function.py): ensure rotation is enabled and the request token identifies a known secret version. Safely return if that version is already `AWSCURRENT`; otherwise, require `AWSPENDING`. Before changing credentials, validate the current credential and confirm that the pending version targets the intended database and user under the chosen rotation strategy. These checks prevent the privileged function from being redirected to another resource. Test the pending credential before promoting its version to `AWSCURRENT`.
-
-These examples demonstrate how you can create architectures that not only manage secrets securely but also automate the rotation process, significantly reducing the risk of compromised credentials.
-
-### 2.5 Handling Secrets in Memory
-
-An additional level of security can be achieved by minimizing the time window
-where a secret is in memory and limiting the access to its memory space.
-
-Depending on your application's particular circumstances, this can be difficult
-to implement in a manner that ensures memory security. Because of this potential
-implementation complexity, you are first encouraged to develop a threat model in order to clearly
-surface your implicit assumptions about both your application's deployment environment as well
-as understand the capabilities of your adversaries.
-

-because as you evaluate a threat model, the potential threat

-exposing secrets in memory. Also, it should be kept in mind while developing an

-the process handling the secret, by that time a security breach may have already

-memory from these types of attacks. This becomes especially important when your
-application is deployed to the cloud. The only foolproof approach to protecting memory
-against these and similar attacks is to fully physically isolate your process memory from all other
-untrusted processes.
-
-Despite the implementation difficulties, in highly sensitive
-environments, protecting secrets in memory can
-be a valuable additional layer of security. For example, in scenarios where an
-advanced attacker can cause a system to crash and gain access to a memory dump,
-they may be able to extract secrets from it. Therefore, carefully safeguarding
-secrets in memory is recommended for untrusted environments or situations where
-tight security is of utmost importance.
-
-Furthermore, in lower-level languages like C/C++, it is relatively easy to protect
-secrets in memory. Thus, it may be worthwhile to implement this practice even if
-the risk of an attacker gaining access to the memory is low. On the other hand, for
