-generally is much more difficult.
-
-- **Structures and Classes:** In .NET and Java, do not use immutable structures
-    such as Strings to store secrets, since it is impossible to force them to
-    be garbage collected. Instead, use primitive types such as byte arrays or
-    char arrays, where the memory can be directly overwritten.
-

-  should be zeroed out to prevent it from lingering in memory where it could
-  potentially be accessed.
-
-- **Memory Encryption:** In some cases, it may be possible to use hardware or
-  operating system features to encrypt the entire memory space of the process
-  handling the secret. This can provide an additional layer of security.
-
-Remember, the goal is to minimize the time window where the secret is in
-plaintext in memory as much as possible.
-
-For more detailed information, see
-[Testing Memory for Sensitive Data](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/tests/android/MASVS-STORAGE/MASTG-TEST-0011)
-from the OWASP MAS project.

-### 2.6 Auditing
-
-Auditing is an essential part of secrets management due to the nature of the application. You must implement auditing securely to be resilient against attempts to tamper with or delete the audit logs. At a minimum, you should audit the following:
+Automated rotation must update credentials without interrupting active workloads:
 
-- Who requested a secret and for what system and role.
-- Whether the secret request was approved or rejected.
-- When the secret was used and by whom/what.
-- When the secret has expired.
-- Whether there were any attempts to reuse expired secrets.
-- If there have been any authentication or authorization errors.
-- When the secret was updated and by whom/what.
-- Any administrative actions and possible user activity on the underlying supporting infrastructure stack.
+- **Dual-Credential Phased Rotation:** For services supporting multiple active credentials (such as API keys, cryptographic verification keys, or database accounts), introduce the new credential while maintaining the previous credential for verification or read operations. Once all clients transition to the new credential, decommission and revoke the old credential.
+- **Orchestrated Multi-Step Rotation:** For target services supporting only one active credential per identity, automated rotation must execute an orchestrated, multi-step sequence rather than an immediate in-place overwrite. The rotation orchestrator (such as a cloud function or controller; see [Choosing a Secret Management Service](#41-choosing-a-secret-management-service)) creates a new pending credential, updates the target service to accept it, tests authentication against the service with the pending credential, and then promotes the pending credential to active before invalidating the prior version.

+Sidecars and local agents (such as Vault Agent or Kubernetes secrets sidecars) serve as client delivery mechanisms that continuously fetch updated or refreshed secrets from the vault into local in-memory mounts without requiring application code changes or restarts (see [Short-Lived Sidecar Containers](#52-short-lived-sidecar-containers)).
 
-### 2.7 Secret Lifecycle
-
-Secrets follow a lifecycle. The stages of the lifecycle are as follows:
-
-- Creation
-- Rotation
-- Revocation
-- Expiration
-
-#### 2.7.1 Creation
-
-New secrets must be securely generated and cryptographically robust enough for their purpose. Secrets must have the minimum privileges assigned to them to enable their required use/role.
+### 2.5 Handling Secrets in Memory
 
-You should transmit credentials securely, such that ideally, you don't send the password along with the username when requesting user accounts. Instead, you should send the password via a secure channel (e.g., mutually authenticated connection) or a side-channel such as push notification, SMS, email. Refer to the [Multi-Factor Authentication Cheat Sheet](Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md) to learn about the pros and cons of each channel.
+Protecting secrets in memory minimizes the exposure window during which plaintext credentials reside in process memory. In-memory defenses protect against credential extraction from crash reports, core dumps, unencrypted swap or paging files, and unauthorized local process inspection. They cannot defend against an attacker with root or kernel access on the host; where untrusted host environments or hypervisors are part of the threat model, deploy hardware-isolated enclaves (see [Confidential Computing and Enclaves](#413-confidential-computing-and-enclaves)).
 
-Applications may not benefit from having multiple communication channels, so you must provision credentials securely.
+Implementation approaches depend on the runtime environment:
 
-See [the Open CRE project on secrets lookup](https://www.opencre.org/cre/223-780) for more technical recommendations on secret creation.
+- **Unmanaged Runtimes (C/C++):** Use explicit secure zeroing functions (`memset_s()`, `explicit_bzero()`, `SecureZeroMemory()`) to overwrite memory buffers immediately after use, preventing compilers from optimizing away the zeroing operation as dead code.
+- **Managed Runtimes (Java, .NET, Go):** Avoid immutable string types (`String`) for sensitive credentials, as they remain in the managed heap until garbage collection occurs and cannot be overwritten in place. Instead, store secrets in mutable primitive arrays (`char[]` or `byte[]`) and explicitly overwrite them (`Arrays.fill()`) immediately after consumption. However, developers must recognize that managed runtimes may create internal copies or relocate objects during garbage collection compaction, JIT compilation, or I/O operations without developer visibility, so reliable zeroization in managed environments cannot always be guaranteed.
+- **Operating System Safeguards:** Disable core dumps (`RLIMIT_CORE` limits or setting the process non-dumpable flag) and lock sensitive memory pages where supported to prevent credentials from being flushed to unencrypted swap or crash artifacts.
 
-#### 2.7.2 Rotation
+For mobile and client-side memory testing methodologies, see [Testing Memory for Sensitive Data](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/tests/android/MASVS-STORAGE/MASTG-TEST-0011) from the OWASP MAS project.
 
-You should regularly rotate secrets so that any stolen credentials will only work for a short time. Regular rotation will also reduce the tendency for users to fall back to bad habits such as reusing credentials.
+### 2.6 Auditing
 
-Depending on a secret's function and what it protects, the lifetime could be from minutes (think end-to-end encrypted chats with perfect forward secrecy) to years (consider hardware secrets).
+Comprehensive, tamper-resistant auditing of the secrets management system is essential for detecting unauthorized access, policy violations, and credential compromise. Audit logs must capture:
 
-User credentials are excluded from regular rotation. These should only be rotated if there is suspicion or evidence that they have been compromised, according to [NIST recommendations](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b05).
+- Secret access requests, approvals, and rejections, recording the requesting identity, target resource, and role.
+- Secret creation, updates, manual or automated rotations, and revocations.
+- Authorization and authentication errors, abnormal access patterns, or attempts to access expired credentials.
+- Administrative actions, policy modifications, and underlying infrastructure events.
 
-#### 2.7.3 Revocation
+Audit logs must use synchronized timestamps generated by secure time-synchronization protocols (such as authenticated NTP) to ensure reliable forensic reconstruction. Protect audit logs against unauthorized modification or deletion, and forward them promptly to a centralized, monitored log repository.
 
-When secrets are no longer required or potentially compromised, you must securely revoke them to restrict access. With (TLS) certificates, this also involves certificate revocation.
+### 2.7 Secret Lifecycle
 
-#### 2.7.4 Expiration
+Secrets must be managed systematically across their operational lifecycle:
 
-You should create secrets to expire after a defined time where possible. This expiration can either be active expiration by the secret consuming system, or an expiration date set at the secrets management system forcing supporting processes to be triggered, resulting in a secret rotation.
-You should apply policies through the secrets management solution to ensure credentials are only made available for a limited time appropriate for the type of credentials. Applications should verify that the secret is still active before trusting it.
+- **Creation:** Generate secrets using cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators (CSPRNG) with sufficient entropy and appropriate key lengths for their cryptographic purpose. Scope newly created credentials to the minimum privileges required. For secret creation recommendations, see [the Open CRE project on secrets lookup](https://www.opencre.org/cre/223-780).
+- **Distribution:** Provision secrets directly to authorized workloads over encrypted transport channels (TLS) or through platform injection mechanisms (such as in-memory volume mounts or environment configurations). Never transmit credentials across unencrypted or out-of-band channels like email or SMS.
+- **Rotation:** Regularly rotate machine credentials and API keys through automated workflows to limit the validity window of compromised secrets. +- **Revocation:** Explicitly and immediately revoke secrets when they are no longer required, when associated workloads are decommissioned, or upon any suspicion of compromise. Certificate management must include corresponding certificate revocation workflows.
+- **Expiration:** Enforce explicit validity bounds and time-to-live (TTL) leases on all issued credentials. Applications and consuming services should verify that a secret is currently active before accepting it, triggering renewal or automated rotation when approaching expiration.

-Never transmit secrets via plaintext. In this day and age, there is no excuse given the ubiquitous adoption of TLS.
+Never transmit secrets in plaintext. Enforce modern Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3) with forward secrecy (such as ECDHE cipher suites) and strict server certificate validation for all secrets management APIs and client connections. Prefer TLS 1.3 where supported, and explicitly prohibit deprecated protocols (SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) and weak ciphers.
 
-Furthermore, you can effectively use secrets management solutions to provision TLS certificates.
+Where zero-trust architectures warrant cryptographic client identity verification at the transport layer, deploy Mutual TLS (mTLS). -Consider the possibility that a secrets management service becomes unavailable for various reasons, such as scheduled downtime for maintenance. Thus, choose maintenance windows carefully based on earlier metrics and audit logs.

-Next, the backup and restore procedures of the system should be regularly tested and audited for their security. A few requirements regarding backup & restore. Ensure that:
+Secrets management systems require robust business continuity and disaster-recovery procedures:
 
-- An automated backup procedure is in place and executed periodically; base the frequency of the backups and snapshots on the number of secrets and their lifecycle.
-- Frequently test restore procedures to guarantee that the backups are intact.
-- Encrypt backups and put them on secure storage with reduced access rights. Monitor the backup location for (unauthorized) access and administrative actions.
-

+- **Restoration Drills:** Regularly test backup restoration procedures in an isolated environment to verify backup integrity and validate recovery time objectives.
+- **Secure Backup Storage:** Encrypt backups at rest, restrict storage access permissions, and monitor the backup location for unauthorized access attempts.
+- **Break-Glass Emergency Access:** Maintain documented, audited emergency procedures to restore service if primary authentication or secrets services fail. Store emergency break-glass credentials in an independent, secondary secrets management system or secure offline custody to eliminate circular dependencies during disaster recovery, and routinely test break-glass access workflows.
 
 ### 2.10 Policies
 
-Consistently enforce policies defining the minimum complexity requirements of passwords and approved encryption algorithms at an organization-wide level. Using a centralized secrets management solution can help companies implement these policies.
-
-Next, having an organization-wide secrets management policy can help enforce applying the best practices defined in this cheat sheet.
+Consistently enforce organization-wide policies defining approved encryption algorithms, key lengths, password complexity rules, and mandatory secrets lifecycle controls. Centralized secrets management solutions provide the technical enforcement mechanism to apply these policies uniformly across development, operational, and cloud environments.
 
 ### 2.11 Metadata: prepare to move the secret
 
-A secret management solution should provide the capability to store at least the following metadata about a secret:
+A secrets management solution should track essential metadata for each managed secret:
 
-- When it was created/consumed/archived/rotated/deleted
-- Who created/consumed/archived/rotated/deleted it (e.g., both the actual producer and the engineer using the production method)
-- What created/consumed/archived/rotated/deleted it
-- Who to contact when having trouble with the secret or having questions about it
-- For what the secret is used (e.g., designated intended consumers and purpose of the secret)
-- What type of secret it is (e.g., AES Key, HMAC key, RSA private key)
-- When you need to rotate it, if done manually
+- **Ownership and Contact:** Technical owner, responsible team, and designated emergency contact.
+- **Purpose and Scope:** Consuming applications, target systems, environments, and business purpose.
+- **Cryptographic Details:** Secret type (e.g., symmetric key, asymmetric key pair, database credential, API token) and algorithm parameters.
+- **Lifecycle Timestamps:** Creation, last consumption, modification, archive, and scheduled rotation dates.
 
-Note: if you don't store metadata about the secret nor prepare to move, you will increase the probability of vendor lock-in.
+Structured metadata facilitates security audits, ownership transitions, automated rotation, and provider migrations to mitigate vendor lock-in.
 
 ### 2.12 Passwordless Authentication and Token Security

review_comments.body:
🤖 _Custodes LLM suggestion: please double-check._

Corrects cutover semantics while preserving key-retention and privileged-rotation safeguards.

````suggestion
Design automated rotation to minimize disruption and handle partial failures:

- **Dual-Credential Phased Rotation:** For services supporting multiple active authentication credentials, introduce the new credential, migrate consumers within a bounded transition period, and revoke the old credential. For cryptographic keys, stop using the old key for new encryption or signing, but retain keys needed to decrypt retained data or verify existing signatures under appropriate access restrictions and retention and compromise-response policies. Client migration alone does not make historical keys safe to delete.
- **Orchestrated Multi-Step Rotation:** For target services supporting only one active credential per identity, create a pending credential, update the target service, test authentication, and promote the tested version in the secrets store. Before changing credentials, validate that the rotation request and pending version are authorized and target the intended service and identity. Handle repeated or already-completed requests safely. Updating the target invalidates the previous credential immediately, so coordinate consumer refresh and define retry and recovery behavior for failures between steps. This sequence alone does not guarantee uninterrupted authentication; use overlapping credentials or separate identities where supported when continuity is required.
````

review_comments.body:
🤖 _Custodes LLM suggestion: please double-check._

Distinguishes secret delivery from backing-service rotation and application reload.

````suggestion
Sidecars and local agents can deliver secrets from a secrets manager into access-restricted, shared in-memory mounts. Long-running agents can refresh delivered secrets when configured to do so; fetch-and-terminate containers provide only initial delivery (see [Short-Lived Sidecar Containers](#52-short-lived-sidecar-containers)). Delivery does not itself rotate credentials at the backing service or update credentials cached by applications. Consumers must support reloading refreshed secrets and updating connections, or require a coordinated restart.
````

🤖 _Custodes LLM suggestion: please double-check._

Limits expiration guidance to enforceable mechanisms and preserves the human-password exception.

````suggestion
- **Expiration:** Use short, explicit validity periods for machine credentials where supported, with expiration enforced by the accepting service or revocation performed by the issuing system. A secrets-store TTL alone does not invalidate a credential at the backing service. Coordinate renewal or rotation before expiration and monitor failures. Do not impose arbitrary periodic expiration on human passwords.
````

Qualifies environment-based delivery without implying that every out-of-band channel is insecure.

````suggestion
- **Distribution:** Provision secrets directly to authorized workloads over encrypted Transport Layer Security (TLS) channels or through access-restricted platform injection mechanisms, such as in-memory volume mounts. Avoid environment variables when safer delivery mechanisms are available, because they can expose secrets through process inspection, logs, or dumps. Never transmit credentials through unencrypted channels or ordinary email or SMS.
````

items.title: Update: Docker Security Cheat Sheet
items.author: SkillDMonkey
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

Rule #5a ("Be careful when mapping container ports to the host with firewalls like UFW") recommends, as Option 1, binding the host side of a published port to `127.0.0.1` (`-p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000`, and the same in Compose). This works for `docker run` and plain Compose, but it is not available for Swarm services (`docker service create --publish`, `docker stack deploy`): a service port cannot be assigned to a single host IP ([moby/moby#26696](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/26696), open since 2016). With the default ingress routing mesh the published port listens on all interfaces of every node in the swarm, not only on the node that runs the task ([Docker docs, routing mesh](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/ingress/): "The routing mesh listens on the published port for any IP address assigned to the node").

A Swarm user who follows Option 1 believes the port is closed while it is reachable on every node.

## How should this be resolved?

Add a short note under Rule #5a for Swarm users:

- Option 1 does not apply to Swarm services; a service published through the routing mesh is reachable on every node and every interface.
- If a service only needs to be reached by other services, do not publish it: attach it to an overlay network (optionally `internal`) and reach it by service name.
- `mode=host` does not help either: it bypasses the routing mesh, but the long `--publish` syntax still has no host IP, so the port opens on all interfaces of the node that runs the task.
- If it must be published, the only control is the host firewall, in the `DOCKER-USER` chain ([Docker docs, packet filtering](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/packet-filtering-firewalls/)).

Single file, a few added lines. We are happy to be assigned and to open the pull request referencing this issue.

AI disclosure: this issue was written and submitted by an AI agent (Claude Opus 5.5) on behalf of Unitizy, with the owner's permission. A second agent checked every claim against the Docker documentation and the moby issue linked above. The limitation was observed on our own Swarm nodes.

items.title: Update: User Privacy Protection Cheat Sheet
items.author: thomas-bartlett
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The [Digital Certificate Pinning](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/User_Privacy_Protection_Cheat_Sheet.html#digital-certificate-pinning) section has not been substantively updated since it was migrated from the OWASP wiki in 2019, and it now conflicts with both the [Pinning Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Pinning_Cheat_Sheet.html#when-do-you-perform-pinning) (revised in #1443) and current browser support.

- The section presents pinning in a "web browser, mobile app or browser plugin" and lists only its advantages. The Pinning Cheat Sheet says there is "almost no situation" where pinning should be considered, since the risk of outages almost always outweighs the security risk it addresses, and: "If it is not a native mobile application, do not pin."
- The section cites [RFC 7469](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7469), which defines HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP), the header websites used to have browsers pin their keys. The RFC has not been obsoleted, but browsers removed support for it ([Chrome 72](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-72-deps-rems), [Firefox 72](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1412438)), so web developers, this cheat sheet's audience, can no longer pin in browsers.

## How should this be resolved?

- Align the section with the Pinning Cheat Sheet: pinning is rarely appropriate, is limited to native mobile applications, and risks outages when certificates or keys change.
- Note that websites can no longer have browsers pin their keys (browsers apply only the pins their vendors build in), and remove the RFC 7469 reference or mark it as historical.

I may be missing context on why the section is scoped this way. I would be happy to submit a PR if helpful.

items.title: Update: [Bot Management and Anti-Automation Cheat Sheet]
items.author: MadEyE355
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Device and Network Fingerprinting section of the Bot Management and Anti-Automation Cheat Sheet covers privacy-aware fingerprint collection, but it could better explain the limitations of using fingerprints for bot detection.

There are three areas that I think would benefit from clarification:

- **Spoofing:** Fingerprint attributes reported by browsers and clients can be manipulated or overridden. This means fingerprints cannot reliably distinguish bots from legitimate users on their own.
- **Collisions:** Different devices or browser environments can produce identical or similar fingerprints. Treating a match as proof of the same device can lead to false positives.
- **Fingerprint drift:** Fingerprints can change over time due to browser updates, operating system changes, hardware changes, and privacy settings. This can make previously stored fingerprints unreliable.

Without mentioning these limitations, developers may place too much trust in fingerprinting results when making bot detection decisions.

## How should this be resolved?

I propose adding a short subsection to the existing Device and Network Fingerprinting section covering these three limitations.

The addition would briefly explain how spoofing, collisions, and fingerprint drift affect fingerprint-based detection, along with practical recommendations:

- Treat fingerprints as one signal among several rather than as definitive evidence of bot activity.
- Avoid blocking users based solely on fingerprint matches.
- Account for partial matches and changes in fingerprints over time.
- Apply appropriate expiration periods to stored fingerprints.

The update would remain brief and follow the existing style of the Cheat Sheet. I would also cross-reference the Authentication Cheat Sheet's guidance on using device fingerprints as risk signals rather than as substitutes for authentication, instead of repeating that guidance.

Related discussion: #2919

## Summary

This PR introduces a new **Service Hardening Cheat Sheet**  addressing OWASP Cheat Sheet Series issue #2856.
The Cheat Sheet provides general service-hardening guidance, practical systemd examples, and an overview of complementary Linux security mechanisms.

## Content Added

- **Introduction and Scope:** Defines the purpose, intended audience, and boundaries of the guidance.
- **General Service Hardening Principles:** Covers software updates, least privilege, attack-surface reduction, secure configurations, network restrictions, credentials and sensitive data, logging and monitoring, resource consumption, and validation.
- **Hardening Services with systemd:** Documents seven hardening directives (`User=`, `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `CapabilityBoundingSet=`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `StateDirectory=`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, and `ProtectHome=yes`), an illustrative service unit, and commands for applying and checking configuration changes.
- **Other Options:** Briefly introduces AppArmor, SELinux, firewalls and network namespaces, Firejail, Landlock, eBPF-based security controls, and containers.
- **References:** Includes supporting documentation and relevant OWASP Cheat Sheets, with control-specific references placed alongside applicable recommendations.

## Testing

+# Service Hardening Cheat Sheet
+
+## Introduction and Scope
+
+Services are software components that perform tasks for applications, users, or other systems. They may process network requests, execute scheduled jobs, access databases, or perform background operations. A service can become an entry point for an attacker if it exposes unnecessary functionality, runs with excessive privileges, or has access to resources beyond those required for its operation.
+
+Service hardening reduces this exposure by restricting a service's privileges, accessible resources, network connectivity, and available functionality. The objective is to reduce opportunities for exploitation and limit the impact of a compromised service.
+
+This Cheat Sheet provides general service-hardening recommendations for developers, system administrators, and DevOps engineers. The principles apply across operating systems where equivalent security controls are available. Their implementation depends on the operating system, service manager, application requirements, and deployment environment.
+
+The Cheat Sheet covers:
+
+- General principles for configuring and operating services securely.
+- Practical hardening of Linux services managed by systemd.
+- Brief references to complementary hardening mechanisms.
+
+The systemd section focuses on host-managed Linux services. Its configuration directives are not directly applicable to other service managers or operating systems.
+
+Container and orchestration security are outside the primary scope. For those environments, refer to the [OWASP Docker Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Docker_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [OWASP Kubernetes Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Kubernetes_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html).
+
+Hardening controls should be selected according to the service's required functionality and threat model. A restriction that is appropriate for one service may prevent another service from operating correctly. Test configuration changes before deploying them to production.
+
+## General Service Hardening Principles
+
+The following recommendations apply to services regardless of the service manager used. Use the equivalent controls provided by the target platform, and verify that the configured restrictions are enforced.
+
+### Keep Service Software and Dependencies Updated
+
+Known vulnerabilities in service software, operating systems, and dependencies can expose services to compromise.
+
+- Use supported versions of the operating system, service software, and dependencies. Maintain an inventory of service components and their versions, using an SBOM where appropriate.
+- Monitor relevant security advisories, prioritize updates according to risk and exposure, and obtain updates from trusted sources using supported authenticity checks.
+
+See the [OWASP Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Vulnerable_Dependency_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html) for detailed guidance on identifying, monitoring, and managing vulnerable dependencies.
+
+### Apply the Principle of Least Privilege
+
+A service should have only the permissions necessary to perform its intended functions. Excessive privileges can increase the impact of a vulnerability or compromised service.
+
+- Run services under dedicated, non-administrative identities where possible, and avoid granting unnecessary capabilities or privileged group memberships.
+- Avoid sharing service identities between unrelated applications when separate identities are practical.
+- Restrict read, write, and execute permissions on files, directories, and other resources.
+
+See the [OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) for additional guidance on least privilege and access control.
+See [systemd.exec(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html) for the `User=`, `Group=`, and `CapabilityBoundingSet=` directives used to restrict service identities and Linux capabilities.
+
+### Reduce the Attack Surface
+
+Every unnecessary interface, component, or enabled feature can introduce additional opportunities for attack.
+
+- Disable service features, plugins, modules, and administrative interfaces that are not required.
+- Disable unnecessary services and background processes.
+- Avoid exposing debugging, diagnostic, or development endpoints in production.
+
+See the [OWASP Attack Surface Analysis Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Attack_Surface_Analysis_Cheat_Sheet.html) for guidance on identifying and reducing exposed functionality and attack surfaces.
+
+### Maintain Secure Service Configurations
+
+Default configurations may enable functionality or access that is unnecessary for a particular deployment. Define and maintain a configuration baseline appropriate to the service.
+
+- Review security-relevant defaults before deployment, including disabling unused default accounts and changing or disabling insecure default credentials.
+- Restrict modification of service configuration files to authorized identities.
+- Keep configuration changes under version control or another auditable change-management process, where practical.
+
+See [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-6 (Configuration Settings)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final) for guidance on establishing, implementing, and monitoring security-relevant configuration settings.
+
+### Restrict Network Communication
+
+A service should accept and initiate only the network connections required for its operation.
+
+- Prefer Unix domain sockets (`AF_UNIX`/`PF_LOCAL`) for local inter-process communication where supported. Otherwise, bind services intended only for local access to the loopback interface rather than exposing them on external network interfaces.
+- Restrict inbound traffic to required ports, protocols, and authorized sources.
+- Restrict outbound connectivity where supported and operationally feasible.
+
+See the [OWASP Network Segmentation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Network_Segmentation_Cheat_Sheet.html) for detailed guidance on restricting network communication and isolating services.
+
+### Protect Service Credentials and Sensitive Data
+
+Services frequently use API keys, database credentials, certificates, and other sensitive information. Exposure of these secrets can allow unauthorized access to the service or dependent systems.
+
+- Do not hardcode secrets in source code or commit them to version control. Provide credentials through an appropriate secrets-management mechanism.
+- Limit access to secrets and the permissions they grant to the service identities and processes that require them.
+- Avoid exposing secrets through command-line arguments, logs, error messages, or other interfaces where they may be disclosed. Prefer secrets-management mechanisms that do not expose credentials through environment variables where practical.
+
+For implementation and credential lifecycle guidance, see the [OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).
+
+### Enable Security-Relevant Logging and Monitoring
+
+Logs and monitoring provide information needed to identify service failures, investigate suspicious activity, and support incident response.
+
+- Record security-relevant service events, such as authentication attempts, access-control failures, and significant configuration changes, with sufficient context for investigation.
+- Avoid logging credentials or unnecessary sensitive information. Protect logs against unauthorized access, modification, and deletion, and handle untrusted log data safely.
+- Monitor service failures, unexpected restarts, unusual resource consumption, and logging failures. Define retention and alerting requirements and verify that important events can be retrieved.
+
+See the [OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html) for detailed logging, protection, retention, and monitoring guidance.
+
+### Limit Resource Consumption
+
+A service that consumes excessive memory, CPU time, processes, or other resources can affect its own availability and that of other workloads.
+
+- Identify the service's expected resource requirements under normal and peak load.
+- Configure resource limits using controls supported by the operating system or service manager.
+- Test limits under representative workloads, including expected peak conditions.
+
+See the [OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Denial_of_Service_Cheat_Sheet.html) for guidance on mitigating resource-exhaustion and denial-of-service risks and [systemd.resource-control(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html) for service-level resource limits using `MemoryMax=` and `TasksMax=`.
+
+## Hardening Services with systemd
+
+On Linux systems using systemd, service unit settings can restrict a service's privileges and access to system resources. Apply restrictions according to the service's requirements, and test them before deployment. These settings provide defense in depth; they do not replace secure application configuration, patching, or other operating-system security controls.
+
+### Apply Least Privilege and Filesystem Restrictions
+
+The following directives are useful starting points for services that support them:
+
+| Directive | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `User=` | Run the service under a dedicated, non-root account rather than as root. |
+| `NoNewPrivileges=yes` | Set the kernel's `no_new_privs` restriction for the service and its descendants, preventing privilege gains through mechanisms such as set-user-ID binaries and file capabilities during program execution. |
+| `CapabilityBoundingSet=` | Restrict the Linux capabilities available to the service. An empty value removes all capabilities from the bounding set. |
+| `ProtectSystem=strict` | Make most of the filesystem hierarchy read-only within the service's mount namespace, subject to documented exceptions and additional writable paths. |
+| `StateDirectory=` | Create and manage a service state directory under `/var/lib`, with write access even when `ProtectSystem=strict` is enabled. |
+| `PrivateTmp=yes` | Give the service private `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` directories, separate from the host's corresponding directories. |
+| `ProtectHome=yes` | Make `/home`, `/root`, and `/run/user` inaccessible within the service's filesystem namespace. |
+
+For example, a service that does not require root privileges, Linux capabilities, or access to home directories might use the following settings in its unit configuration:
+
+```ini
+[Service]
+User=example-service
+NoNewPrivileges=yes
+CapabilityBoundingSet=
+ProtectSystem=strict
+StateDirectory=example-service
+PrivateTmp=yes
+ProtectHome=yes
+```
+
+This is an **illustrative configuration, not a universal baseline**. The service account must exist, and the restrictions must be compatible with the application's actual requirements. An empty capability bounding set can break operations requiring Linux capabilities. Filesystem restrictions can also prevent access to required configuration, data, sockets, or other resources.
+
+Prefer explicitly managed writable directories, such as `StateDirectory=`, over granting broad write access. If the service needs additional writable paths, evaluate narrowly scoped exceptions rather than disabling filesystem protection altogether.
+
+`ProtectSystem=strict` restricts filesystem writes but does not prevent reading accessible files. The `/dev`, `/proc`, and `/sys` subtrees are excluded from its read-only protection. Additional controls may be needed to restrict access to these resources. Writable-directory exceptions and other filesystem namespace limitations must also be considered.
+
+See the [systemd.exec manual](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.exec.html) for directive semantics, exceptions, and interactions.
+
+### Restrict Network Communication
+
+systemd can restrict the network address families and IP destinations available to a service.
+
+| Directive | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `RestrictAddressFamilies=` | Restrict the socket address families a service can create, such as `AF_UNIX`, `AF_INET`, and `AF_INET6`. Allow only those required by the service. |
+| `IPAddressDeny=` / `IPAddressAllow=` | Restrict inbound and outbound IPv4 and IPv6 traffic using denied and permitted address ranges. |
+
+`RestrictAddressFamilies=` does not restrict sockets passed to a service through socket activation. IP address filtering requires supported kernel functionality and may have no effect where the necessary eBPF support is unavailable. For socket-activated services, configure appropriate IP restrictions on both the socket and service units.
+
+See [systemd.exec(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html) and [systemd.resource-control(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html) for network restriction options and their limitations.
+
+### Restrict System Calls
+
+systemd can restrict the system calls available to a service using seccomp filtering.
+
+| Directive | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `SystemCallFilter=@system-service` | Apply a system-call allowlist using the `@system-service` group. System calls outside the permitted set are blocked, subject to systemd's filtering behavior and exceptions. |
+
+This filter is suitable for consideration by many system services, but it can prevent applications from using required system calls. Test compatibility before enabling it. By default, prohibited system calls cause the affected process to receive `SIGSYS`.
+
+See [systemd.exec(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html) for system-call filtering behavior and supported system-call groups.
+
+### Limit Service Resource Consumption
+
+systemd can use Linux control groups to limit resources consumed by a service.
+
+| Directive | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| `MemoryMax=` | Set an absolute memory usage limit for the service. Exceeding the limit can trigger out-of-memory termination within the unit. |
+| `TasksMax=` | Limit the number of tasks, including processes and threads, that the service can create. |
+
+Select limits based on the service's expected workload and test them under representative conditions. `MemoryMax=` is a final safeguard rather than a substitute for appropriate memory management; `MemoryHigh=` is recommended as the primary memory-control mechanism.
+
+See [systemd.resource-control(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html) for resource limits and control-group requirements.
+
+### Protect Service Credentials
+
+Do not pass secrets through `Environment=` or `EnvironmentFile=`. systemd warns that environment variables may be exposed through D-Bus IPC and inherited by processes that should not receive them.
+
+Use `LoadCredential=` to provide credentials through a restricted, read-only credential directory instead. The service must be configured to read the supplied credential files.
+
+See [systemd.exec(5): Credentials](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html#Credentials) for credential-loading options and their security properties.
+
+### Apply and Validate Changes
+
+Use a service-specific drop-in rather than editing a package-managed unit file directly:
+
+```bash
+sudo systemctl edit example.service
+```
+
+Add only the directives appropriate for that service. Saving changes through `systemctl edit` normally reloads the systemd manager configuration automatically. If unit files or drop-ins are modified manually, reload the configuration before restarting the service:
+
+```bash
+sudo systemctl daemon-reload
+```
+
+Restart the service and inspect its status and logs:
+
+```bash
+sudo systemctl restart example.service
+systemctl status example.service
+journalctl -u example.service --no-pager
+```
+
+Verify that the service still performs its required operations, including reading necessary files, writing persistent state, and handling expected requests. Where possible, test the relevant restriction directly: compare access or behavior before and after enabling a directive, while keeping other conditions unchanged.
+
+The following command provides an additional review of a unit's sandboxing and security-related settings:
+
+```bash
+systemd-analyze security example.service
+```
+
+Its exposure score is a **heuristic assessment of unit settings**, not proof that the service is secure or vulnerable. It does not replace functional testing, application review, or verification of the effective restrictions.
+
+Consult the [systemd-analyze manual](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd-analyze.html) and the [systemctl manual](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemctl.html) for further details.
+
+Review hardening settings when service requirements change, and validate compatibility with the systemd version and Linux kernel used in the deployment.
+
+## Other Options
+
+Service hardening can also use controls outside systemd. The appropriate mechanisms depend on the operating system, deployment environment, and service requirements. These controls can complement one another, but each must be configured and validated for the service being protected.
+
+### AppArmor and SELinux
+
+AppArmor and SELinux are Linux mandatory access control (MAC) mechanisms that can restrict what a service is permitted to access or perform, beyond traditional file permissions.
+
+For AppArmor, apply an appropriate enforced profile to the service. Processes without an applicable profile may run unconfined. For SELinux, use an enforcing policy and ensure that the service runs in an appropriately confined domain with correct resource labels. An enabled security module does not necessarily mean that a particular service is confined.
+
+See the [Linux kernel AppArmor documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/LSM/apparmor.html) and [Red Hat's SELinux documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/using_selinux/).
+
+### Firewalls and Network Namespaces
+
+Use host or network firewalls to restrict traffic to the ports, protocols, sources, and destinations required by the service. Consider both inbound and outbound traffic according to the service's communication requirements.
+
+On Linux, nftables can apply service-specific outbound traffic restrictions using the `output` chain and socket user identity matching (`meta skuid`). This can help restrict network connections initiated by services running under dedicated user accounts. When multiple services share an account, user-based rules cannot distinguish between them.
+
+Linux network namespaces can provide separate network interfaces, routing tables, and network stacks for services. However, a network namespace alone does not establish an appropriate traffic-filtering policy. Configure and verify network connectivity and firewall rules explicitly.
+
+See the [nftables documentation](https://wiki.nftables.org/wiki-nftables/index.php/Main_Page) and [network_namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/network_namespaces.7.html).
+
+### Application Sandboxing
+
+Application sandboxing tools, such as Firejail, can restrict a service's execution environment using Linux namespaces, seccomp filters, and capability controls.
+
+Evaluate the sandbox's privileges, configuration, security implications, and compatibility before deployment. A sandboxing tool does not automatically provide complete isolation, and some implementations introduce their own privileged components.
+
+See the [Firejail manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/firejail.1.html).
+
+### Landlock
+
+Landlock is a Linux security module that allows processes, including unprivileged processes, to apply additional restrictions to themselves and their descendants.
+
+Developers can use Landlock to limit supported operations on resources such as files. Available restrictions depend on the running kernel and supported Landlock ABI version. Applications should check supported features rather than assume that every restriction is available.
+
+See the [Linux kernel Landlock documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/userspace-api/landlock.html).
+
+### eBPF-Based Security Controls
+
+Security tools built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) can support runtime monitoring and, with appropriate kernel facilities such as BPF LSM, enforcement of security policies.
+
+The protection provided depends on the specific tool, its policies, privileges, and kernel support. eBPF itself is not a security policy, and monitoring alone does not prevent prohibited operations.
+
+See the [Linux kernel BPF LSM documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/bpf/prog_lsm.html).
+
+### Containers
+
+Containers can provide additional isolation for services through Linux namespaces, control groups, and other security mechanisms. However, containerization alone does not guarantee that a service is secure. Apply least privilege, restrict unnecessary capabilities, and avoid privileged containers unless explicitly required.
+
+For Docker-specific hardening guidance, see the [OWASP Docker Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Docker_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html).
+
+## References
+
+- [systemd.exec(5) — Execution Environment Configuration](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html)
+- [systemd.resource-control(5) — Resource Control Unit Settings](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html)
+- [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — Security and Privacy Controls](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final)

items.title: Build an official Cheat Sheet Series skill (v1)
items.author: mackowski
items.body:
## Approved implementation task

Build a documentation-only, skill-first v1, assigned to @mackowski. Follow the [approved scope and acceptance criteria](https://github.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries/issues/2843#issuecomment-6316809175).

The MCP server proposal below is retained as discussion background and is outside the approved v1 scope.

---

## Summary

I'd like to propose an official, read-only [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP) server for the Cheat Sheet Series. It would let AI assistants (Claude, Copilot, Cursor, etc.) retrieve authoritative OWASP guidance on demand instead of relying on whatever they memorized during training, which may be outdated or distorted.

## Motivation

- Developers increasingly ask AI assistants security questions ("how do I store passwords?", "how should I handle CSRF here?").
- Answers from models are often generic, stale, or subtly wrong, and don't point back to the source.
- The Cheat Sheets are concise, practical and maintained, which makes them well suited as a retrieval source.
- An official server would keep the content current and attributed, rather than leaving it to unofficial copies that drift out of date.

## Proposed scope (v1, deliberately small)

Read-only tools, no side effects:

- `list_cheatsheets`: names plus a one-line description
- `get_cheatsheet(name, section?)`: full content or a single section
- `search_cheatsheets(query)`: the most relevant chunks, each with a link to the source page

Optional later: lookup by ASVS requirement / OWASP Top 10 category using the existing index files, and MCP *resources* (`cheatsheet://<name>`) and *prompts*.

## Design notes

- **Source of truth:** the Markdown files in `cheatsheets/`. A CI step builds a search index (chunked by headings, with metadata and canonical URLs) on each merge, so the server never serves stale content.
- **No LLM summarization in v1.** The server returns original passages with context, so the authoritative text is never paraphrased or hallucinated.
- **Attribution:** every response includes the cheat sheet title, URL and license (CC BY-SA 4.0).
- **Transport:** local `stdio` first (simple to run, no hosting). Streamable HTTP can be added later for a hosted instance.
- **Retrieval:** start with plain full-text / BM25 on heading-based chunks; evaluate with a small set of real questions before considering embeddings.

## Security considerations

- Server is read-only and exposes no tools with side effects.
- Cheat sheet content is community-edited Markdown returned to an AI agent as tool output, so it is effectively an indirect prompt injection surface. PR review remains the trust boundary, and responses should be clearly marked as data.
- For any HTTP deployment: rate limiting, `Origin` validation, TLS.

items.author: jmanico
items.body:
## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The XSS Filter Evasion Cheat Sheet is 1,143 lines. Many of its vectors depend on legacy engines. The sheet refers to IE 16 times (VBScript, HTC files, XML data islands, CSS expressions), and it also has Gecko-only tricks like `-moz-binding` and META `Set-Cookie`, which modern browsers ignore.

Some entries are not XSS filter evasion at all: SSI and PHP are server-side execution, and "IMG Embedded Commands" is really CSRF. The BODY event-handler list is about 135 lines and mixes standard events with IE-only ones like `onBounce`.

## How should this be resolved?

- Separate legacy-engine vectors from tests that matter for modern browsers. Edge IE mode still runs Trident for some intranet apps, so IE-only vectors can move into one short legacy section rather than disappear entirely.
- Remove vectors that only worked in engines nobody tests anymore.
- Trim the BODY event-handler list to standard events.
- Drop the entries that aren't XSS filter evasion (SSI, PHP, IMG Embedded Commands).
- Fix the alert-obfuscation examples that use curly quotes.
- Each removal or legacy move should say which browser or engine the vector depended on, so reviewers can check it.

Small PRs, one section at a time, please. They are much easier to review than one big rewrite :)

## What is missing or needs to be updated?

The Multi-Tenant Security Cheat Sheet is 1,063 lines, and 771 of them are code. The design guidance is good, but the sheet carries full implementations we can't maintain. The biggest blocks are lifecycle (about 154 code lines), logging (143), file storage (107), rate limiting (106) and SQLAlchemy (75).

The sheet also never links the IDOR or Logging cheat sheets, and the Do's and Don'ts list restates every section.

## How should this be resolved?

- Keep each of the 8 sections focused on the design decision and its tradeoffs. The RLS guidance (`SET LOCAL`, `BYPASSRLS`, connection reuse) and the backup-restore guidance are the strongest parts, so keep them.
- Cut the long examples down to the smallest snippet that makes the point, or remove them and link to vendor or framework docs.
- Some requirements live only in code today (for example, revoking sessions and API keys at offboarding). Move those into the prose before cutting the code, and fix any prose that explains a removed example.
- Add links to the [IDOR](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [Logging](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html) cheat sheets.
- Shorten the Do's and Don'ts so it doesn't restate every section.

Small PRs, one section at a time, please. They are much easier to review than one big rewrite :)
